q: In what sequence are the Social Combination rules followed for group success?
doubt: If 'equal to the best member' (disjunctive) is ranked above 'better than most members' (compensatory), disjunctive moves to second place, which gives (1).
who: Ivan Steiner, typology of group tasks (1972)

concept.t: This is the standard order of Ivan Steiner's combination rules, from the most to the least group success: additive first, conjunctive last.

Steiner classified tasks by how members' inputs are combined. Additive tasks sum efforts (tug of war), so the group beats its best member; compensatory tasks average judgements, so the group beats most members.
Disjunctive tasks need one correct answer, so the group can only equal its best member. Conjunctive tasks need everyone to finish, so the weakest member sets the pace, like a roped climbing team.
Pooling (additive, compensatory) helps groups most; conjunctive tasks expose the weakest link. Steiner also named discretionary tasks, where the group picks its own rule.

wrong.1: Swaps compensatory and disjunctive; the standard sequence places compensatory (averaging judgements) second and disjunctive (relying on the best member) third.
wrong.3: Reverses the scale by ending with additive; additive tasks, where every member's effort adds up, give the highest group output and come first.
wrong.4: Ends with additive and puts conjunctive second; additive tasks should head the list, and conjunctive tasks, limited by the weakest member, come last.

q: Which mnemonic device is used for the expression of different letters of a word?
who: First-letter mnemonics (acronyms)

concept.t: An acronym takes the first letter of each item to be remembered and makes a word or name from them, so each letter cues one item.
ROY G BIV gives the colours of the spectrum (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet). HOMES gives the five Great Lakes.
Acronym = letters form a word; acrostic = letters begin the words of a sentence; method of loci = familiar places; peg-word = rhyming pegs.

wrong.1: Acoustic coding means storing information by its sound, typical of short-term memory; it is not a memory aid built from letters.
wrong.3: The keyword method links a new (often foreign) word to a similar-sounding familiar word plus a vivid image; it is used for vocabulary learning.
wrong.4: Clustering is grouping items by meaning or category during recall, such as all fruits together; it organises items rather than using their letters.

q: Which of the following was described by R.B. Cattell using P-Technique of Factor Analysis?
who: Raymond Cattell, P-technique factor analysis

concept.t: P-technique factor-analyses many measures taken on one person across many occasions, so it shows how that person's personality shifts with changing situations.
Ordinary R-technique correlates tests across many people, giving individual differences. Q-technique correlates people across tests to find types. P-technique stays inside one individual over time.
Raymond Cattell used P-technique to separate fluctuating states from stable traits. P = Person over occasions; R = many people; Q = people as variables.

wrong.2: Group formation is studied through sociometry and small-group research, not by factor-analysing one person's scores over time.
wrong.3: Patterns of social interaction are mapped by observation methods such as Robert Bales' interaction process analysis, not by P-technique.
wrong.4: Differences between people come from R-technique, which correlates traits across a large sample; P-technique deliberately studies a single person.

q: Which of the following would be the best method for studying the relative contribution of heredity and environment?
who: Twin and adoption designs (behaviour genetics)

concept.t: Using identical and fraternal twins, with half reared apart, varies genes and environment separately, so the effect of each can be pulled apart.

Identical (MZ) twins share all their genes, fraternal (DZ) twins about half. If MZ twins stay more alike than DZ twins even when reared apart, heredity matters; if twins reared together are more alike than those reared apart, shared environment matters.
The fullest design has four groups: MZ together, MZ apart, DZ together, DZ apart. Each comparison isolates one source of similarity.

wrong.1: Twins reared together share their home as well as their genes, so environment never varies; greater MZ similarity could partly reflect more similar treatment.
wrong.2: Separating twins varies environment, but without a reared-together comparison you cannot gauge how much a shared upbringing adds.
wrong.3: Ordinary siblings all share about half their genes, so genetic similarity never varies and the role of heredity cannot be estimated.

q: Which one of the following statements is true regarding the relationship of test length with reliability and validity?
who: Spearman-Brown prophecy formula

concept.t: Adding more comparable items shrinks the share of random error, so reliability rises; because validity is limited by reliability, validity rises too, though more slowly.
The Spearman-Brown formula predicts the new reliability: rnew = nr / [1 + (n - 1)r], where n is how many times longer the test becomes.
A validity coefficient cannot exceed the square root of reliability, so a more reliable test has a higher validity ceiling. Gains level off as a test gets very long.

wrong.1: Validity also improves with length, because the ceiling on validity is set by reliability; reliability does not rise on its own.
wrong.2: Reliability is the quantity most directly raised by lengthening (Spearman-Brown), so it cannot be that only validity improves.
wrong.3: Lengthening with comparable items does improve both; only adding poor or unrelated items fails to help.

q:
Match the given concepts in List I with the description given in List II. 
 
 List I: (a) Turiyavastha; (b) Prajnavastha; (c) Swapanvastha; (d) Jagratavastha

 List II: (i) The state of normal consciousness concerned with the material world; (ii) Subconscious faculty concerned with the subtler aspects of human knowledge and experience; (iii) State of super consciousness when the dichotomy between grossness and subtlety disappears; (iv) Steady state of consciousness when the essential nature of atman is experienced

 
 Codes:
who: Mandukya Upanishad, four states of consciousness

concept.t: (a) Turiyavastha = (iv) steady state where the atman is experienced; (b) Prajnavastha = (iii) super consciousness beyond gross and subtle; (c) Swapanvastha = (ii) subconscious, subtle experience; (d) Jagratavastha = (i) normal waking consciousness of the material world.
The Mandukya Upanishad describes waking (Jagrat), dream (Swapna), deep sleep (Prajna or Sushupti) and the fourth state, Turiya, pure consciousness underlying the other three.
From gross to subtle: Jagrat → Swapna → Prajna → Turiya. Turiya literally means 'the fourth'.

wrong.1: Gives normal waking consciousness (i) to the dream state and the atman state (iv) to Jagrat, reversing the least and most subtle states.
wrong.3: Swaps Turiya and Prajna; the steady experience of the atman belongs to Turiya, the fourth state, not to deep sleep.
wrong.4: Swaps Turiya and Jagrat; Jagrat is ordinary waking awareness of the material world, while Turiya is the state in which the atman is known.

q:
The Eudemonic view of Subjective Well-being holds that: 
 
 (a) true happiness is found in expression of virtue

 (b) well-being refers to "striving for perfection"

 (c) subjective well-being focuses on bodily pleasures like focus on appetite and self-interests

 (d) well-being consists of fulfilling its true self

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Aristotle's eudaimonia; Carol Ryff's psychological well-being

concept.t: The eudaimonic view says well-being comes from living virtuously and realising one's true potential, so (a), (b) and (d) fit.

Aristotle saw happiness as the expression of virtue. Carol Ryff described well-being as striving for perfection that realises one's true potential, and Alan Waterman tied it to living in line with the true self (daimon).
Bodily pleasure, appetite and self-interest describe the hedonic view, which equates well-being with gaining pleasure and avoiding pain.
Hedonic = feeling good (Ed Diener's subjective well-being); eudaimonic = functioning well (Ryff's six dimensions).

wrong.1: Statement (c) is the hedonic view of pleasure and appetite, the opposite of the eudaimonic view.
wrong.2: (d) is eudaimonic, but (c) is hedonic, and the option leaves out (a) and (b), which are core eudaimonic ideas.
wrong.4: (a) is correct, but (b) and (d), striving for perfection and fulfilling the true self, are also eudaimonic, so (a) alone is incomplete.

q: Read the following conversation and choose the best option. X: "What time is it?" Y: "I think it is about 9.30 AM."
who: Eric Berne, transactional analysis

concept.t: X asks a factual question from the Adult to Y's Adult, and Y replies Adult to Adult. The reply comes from the ego state that was addressed, so the transaction is complementary.
In Eric Berne's transactional analysis, a complementary transaction has parallel lines on the diagram: the expected ego state responds, so communication can go on smoothly.
Complementary = expected reply; crossed = reply from an unexpected ego state, which halts communication; ulterior = a hidden psychological message under the social one.

wrong.1: True as far as it goes but incomplete; it leaves out that the transaction is complementary, which is the defining feature here.
wrong.3: Neither speaker is in the Child state; both are calm, factual and reality-focused, which marks the Adult.
wrong.4: X's question is a neutral request for information, not a Child expression of feeling, play or need.

q:
Which are the two basic features of Schema? 
 
 (a) Influencing memory

 (b) Promoting forgetting

 (c) Resisting change

 (d) Promoting change

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Frederic Bartlett; Robert Baron and Donn Byrne, social cognition

concept.t: Schemas influence memory (what we notice, store and recall), and they resist change, even when evidence contradicts them.
Frederic Bartlett's 'War of the Ghosts' study showed people reshaping an unfamiliar story to fit their own cultural schemas when they recalled it.
This stubbornness is the perseverance effect: schemas and beliefs persist even after the information that built them has been discredited.
Schemas can also act as self-fulfilling prophecies, leading people to behave in ways that make the expectation come true.

wrong.1: Influencing memory is right, but promoting forgetting is not a defining feature; the second basic feature is resistance to change.
wrong.3: Schemas do the opposite of promoting change: they are stable and tend to persist against contradicting evidence.
wrong.4: Resisting change is right, but promoting forgetting is not a core feature; the other basic feature is their influence on memory.

q: Which among the following are the levels of processing proposed by Craik and Lockhart?
who: Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart, levels of processing (1972)

concept.t: Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart described processing from shallow to deep: physical (structural, how a word looks), acoustic (phonemic, how it sounds) and semantic (what it means).
Deeper processing gives more durable memory. Judging a word's meaning leads to better recall than judging its rhyme, which beats judging its typeface.
Shallow = structural; middle = phonemic; deep = semantic. Elaborative rehearsal supports deep processing, while maintenance rehearsal keeps it shallow.

wrong.1: Symbolic is not one of the levels; the shallowest level is physical or structural processing of how the stimulus looks.
wrong.2: Behavioural is not a level of processing, and the deepest level, semantic processing of meaning, is missing.
wrong.3: Behavioural is not a level, and the shallow physical (structural) level is missing from this set.

q:
According to Goleman, the 'Management of Emotions' component of Emotional Intelligence includes: 
 
 (a) Handling feelings so that they are appropriate.

 (b) Ability to soothe oneself.

 (c) Ability to shake off rampant anxiety, gloom or irritability.

 (d) Recognizing a feeling as it happens.

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Daniel Goleman, Emotional Intelligence (1995)

concept.t: In Daniel Goleman's model, managing emotions means handling feelings so they are appropriate, soothing oneself and shaking off rampant anxiety, gloom or irritability: (a), (b) and (c).
Recognising a feeling as it happens is knowing one's emotions (self-awareness), the first and separate domain.
Goleman, building on Peter Salovey and John Mayer, lists: knowing one's emotions, managing emotions, motivating oneself, recognising emotions in others and handling relationships.

wrong.1: (d), recognising a feeling as it happens, is self-awareness, not management; and (c), shaking off anxiety or gloom, is left out.
wrong.2: (d) belongs to self-awareness, and the option omits (a), handling feelings so they are appropriate, the core of managing emotions.
wrong.4: (d) does not belong; recognising a feeling as it happens is self-awareness, a separate domain that comes before managing it.

q: Read the following conversation and choose the correct option. X: "I am so hungry! I am like way starving." Y: "You might consider a small nutritional snack to suppress your appetite."
who: Eric Berne, transactional analysis: crossed transaction

concept.t: X speaks from the Child (an excited, needy complaint) to Y's Child. Y answers from the Adult with factual advice aimed at X's Adult, so the transaction is crossed.

In Eric Berne's transactional analysis, a crossed transaction occurs when the reply comes from an ego state other than the one addressed. The lines cross on the diagram and communication breaks down until someone shifts.
Read each line separately: which ego state is speaking and which it is aimed at. Expected reply = complementary; switched states = crossed.

wrong.1: X's excited 'way starving' is not an Adult statement and Y's measured advice is not a Child statement; the labels are reversed.
wrong.2: A complementary reply would come from Y's Child (for example, 'Me too, let's get pizza!'); Y switches to the Adult instead.
wrong.4: Child to Adult answered by Adult to Child gives parallel lines, which is a complementary transaction, so calling it crossed is self-contradictory.

q:
Match the following concepts with the corresponding bodily states. 
 
 List I: (a) Rebound Phenomena; (b) Phantom Limb; (c) Scotopic Process; (d) Apoptosis

 List II: (i) REM sleep; (ii) Pain; (iii) Vision; (iv) Cell death

 
 Choose the correct option from those given below:
who: Biopsychology: sleep, pain, vision and cell death

concept.t: (a) Rebound phenomena = (i) REM sleep; (b) Phantom limb = (ii) pain; (c) Scotopic process = (iii) vision; (d) Apoptosis = (iv) cell death.
REM rebound: after REM deprivation, people show more REM sleep than usual on later nights. Phantom limb: sensations, often pain, felt in a limb that has been amputated.
Scotopic vision is rod-based vision in dim light, without colour. Apoptosis is programmed, active cell death, as when surplus neurons die during development.

wrong.2: Swaps REM sleep and pain between (a) and (b), and links scotopic to cell death; scotopic refers to rod vision in dim light.
wrong.3: Links phantom limb to cell death and apoptosis to pain; phantom limb is a pain sensation, and apoptosis is programmed cell death.
wrong.4: Links rebound to cell death and apoptosis to pain; rebound is the extra REM sleep after REM deprivation.

q: What is the reason for the negative voltage of a neuron during Resting Potential? (Sodium = Na+; Potassium = K+; Chloride = Cl-; Organic anions = A-)
who: Ionic basis of the resting membrane potential

concept.t: At rest, Na+ and Cl- are concentrated outside the neuron, while K+ and A- (large organic anions) are concentrated inside. The inside ends up more negative, about -70 mV.
The organic anions are proteins too large to leave the cell. The membrane leaks K+ out more easily than Na+ in, and the sodium-potassium pump pushes out 3 Na+ for every 2 K+ it brings in.
Inside: K+ and A-. Outside: Na+ and Cl-. The resting potential is about -70 mV, inside relative to outside.

wrong.1: The ion locations are right, but the charge comparison is reversed; the inside, not the outside, is the more negative side.
wrong.3: Organic anions (A<sup>-</sup>) are trapped inside the cell and Cl<sup>-</sup> is concentrated outside, so this ion distribution is wrong.
wrong.4: Puts A<sup>-</sup> outside and Cl<sup>-</sup> inside; in fact the large protein anions stay inside and chloride is mostly outside.

q: Descartes argued that body and mind interact. According to him, which is the site for this interaction?
who: René Descartes, interactionist dualism

concept.t: René Descartes held that the non-physical mind and the mechanical body interact at the pineal gland.
He thought it was the only brain structure that is single rather than paired, so it could unite the double input from the two sides of the body.
Descartes = interactionism; Baruch Spinoza = double aspect theory; Gottfried Leibniz = psychophysical parallelism.

wrong.1: The pancreas is a digestive and endocrine gland that secretes insulin; it plays no part in Descartes' theory.
wrong.3: The pituitary is the master endocrine gland under the hypothalamus, not Descartes' seat of the soul.
wrong.4: The adrenal glands sit on the kidneys and release adrenaline and cortisol in stress; Descartes did not link them to the mind.

q: Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A): Sensitivity to targets reflects the placement of a flexible criterion and is measured in terms of 'hits minus false alarms'. Reason (R): When the consequences of making a Miss are very grave, we lower the criterion for considering something as a 'Hit'. In the light of the above two statements, choose the correct option:
doubt: If the setter reads 'hits minus false alarms' as an acceptable sensitivity index and ignores the criterion clause, A passes as true and (2) would be chosen.
who: David Green and John Swets, signal detection theory

concept.t: False. In signal detection theory, sensitivity (d') reflects how well signal is separated from noise and does not depend on where the criterion is set; criterion placement is response bias (β).
True. When a miss is very costly, such as missing a tumour on an X-ray, observers lower (relax) the criterion and say 'yes' more often, gaining hits at the cost of more false alarms.
Payoffs and expectations move the criterion; stimulus strength and the observer's acuity change d'. Hit rate minus false alarm rate is only a rough sensitivity index.

wrong.1: A is false, because criterion placement reflects bias rather than sensitivity, so R cannot explain it.
wrong.2: A is not true, since sensitivity (d') is independent of where the criterion is placed; only R is correct.
wrong.3: Reversed: A is false, while R is true, since costly misses push observers towards a lower, more lenient criterion.

q: According to definition theory, for the development of a concept of an OFFICE, one must:
who: Classical (defining-attribute) theory of concepts

concept.t: Definition theory (the classical view) says a concept is a list of necessary and sufficient features; anything with all of them belongs, and anything lacking one does not.
Prototype theory (Eleanor Rosch) uses a best or typical example; exemplar theory stores many remembered examples and compares new items with them.
Definition = checklist of essential features; prototype = typical average; exemplar = stored instances. Definition theory struggles with fuzzy categories such as 'game'.

wrong.1: Building an ideal or typical office is prototype theory, where membership depends on similarity to the best example.
wrong.2: Gathering experience of many particular offices fits exemplar theory, which compares new items with stored instances.
wrong.4: Converting a room describes making an office, not how the concept is represented in the mind; no theory of concepts proposes it.

q:
Match the following Intelligence/Ability tests with the associated features. 
 
 List I: (a) Naglieri Non-verbal Ability test; (b) Raven's Progressive Matrices (Standard); (c) Torrance Test of Creative Thinking; (d) Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale

 List II: (i) Provides deviation IQ; (ii) Open-ended test; (iii) Suitable for children; (iv) Adult Culture Fair Test

 
 Choose the correct option from those given below:
who: Jack Naglieri, John Raven, E. Paul Torrance, David Wechsler

concept.t: (a) Naglieri Nonverbal Ability Test = (iii) suitable for children; (b) Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices = (iv) adult culture-fair test; (c) Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking = (ii) open-ended; (d) WAIS = (i) deviation IQ.
Jack Naglieri's test is a non-verbal matrices test for school-age children. John Raven's Standard Matrices suit older children and adults; the Coloured version is for young children.
E. Paul Torrance's tasks are open-ended, scored for fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration. David Wechsler replaced the ratio IQ with the deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15).

wrong.2: Calls Raven's open-ended and gives Torrance the deviation IQ; Raven's items have one right answer, while Torrance's divergent-thinking tasks are open-ended.
wrong.3: Swaps (a) and (b); the Naglieri test is built for school-age children, while the Standard Raven's Matrices is the adult culture-fair test.
wrong.4: Gives Torrance the deviation IQ and the WAIS the open-ended label; the WAIS yields deviation IQ and Torrance's creativity tasks are open-ended.

q: Y has 'concrete experience' and 'reflective observation' as dominant learning abilities, views concrete situations from different viewpoints, has broad cultural interests and is imaginative and emotional. His experiential learning style is:
who: David Kolb, experiential learning theory (1984)

concept.t: David Kolb's diverging style combines concrete experience with reflective observation. Divergers view situations from many angles, brainstorm well, and are imaginative and emotional with broad cultural interests.

Diverging = CE + RO; assimilating = AC + RO; converging = AC + AE; accommodating = CE + AE (CE concrete experience, RO reflective observation, AC abstract conceptualisation, AE active experimentation).
Kolb's learning cycle: concrete experience → reflective observation → abstract conceptualisation → active experimentation. Each style sits between two neighbouring stages.

wrong.1: Assimilators combine abstract conceptualisation and reflective observation; they prefer logical theories and ideas to people and feelings.
wrong.3: Convergers combine abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation; they excel at practical problem-solving and prefer technical tasks to people.
wrong.4: Accommodators combine concrete experience and active experimentation; they learn hands-on, take risks and act on gut feeling.

q:
Match the given concepts with the relevant description. 
 
 List I: (a) Bottom up; (b) Top down; (c) Happiness set point; (d) Hedonic adaptation

 List II: (i) Happiness due to circumstances tends to be temporary because we generally adjust fairly soon to new circumstances; (ii) Life circumstances influence happiness; (iii) Happiness begins in ourselves; (iv) Happiness levels are fixed and stable across time

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Ed Diener; Philip Brickman; David Lykken and Auke Tellegen

concept.t: (a) Bottom up = (ii) life circumstances influence happiness; (b) Top down = (iii) happiness begins in ourselves; (c) Happiness set point = (iv) happiness levels are fixed and stable; (d) Hedonic adaptation = (i) we soon adjust to new circumstances.
Bottom-up theories build happiness from good events and conditions; top-down theories (as reviewed by Ed Diener) say personality and outlook colour how we judge everything.
The set point idea (David Lykken and Auke Tellegen) holds that each person drifts back to a largely inherited baseline. Philip Brickman's studies of lottery winners illustrated hedonic adaptation.

wrong.1: Mismatches (b) and (d): top down means happiness starts in the person, while hedonic adaptation means adjusting to new circumstances.
wrong.2: Swaps (c) and (d): set point means a stable baseline (iv), while hedonic adaptation is the quick adjustment to new circumstances (i).
wrong.3: Swaps bottom up and top down; bottom-up theories trace happiness to life circumstances, while top-down theories start from the person.

q: The bipolar adjectives scale 'Fast……slow' in Osgood's semantic differential would belong to:
who: Charles Osgood, semantic differential (1957)

concept.t: Fast-slow describes motion and liveliness, so it loads on the activity factor.
Charles Osgood found three factors of meaning: evaluation (good-bad, pleasant-unpleasant), potency (strong-weak, heavy-light) and activity (fast-slow, active-passive).
Remember EPA: Evaluation, Potency, Activity. Evaluation accounts for the largest share of variance.

wrong.1: The evaluative factor covers judgements of worth, such as good-bad, nice-awful and pleasant-unpleasant.
wrong.2: The potency factor covers strength and size, such as strong-weak, large-small and heavy-light.
wrong.3: Osgood's semantic differential has no general factor; its three factors are evaluation, potency and activity.

q: Which of the following problem-solving techniques involves the analysis of the difference between the current situation and the desired set goal, then doing something to reduce this difference?
who: Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, means-end analysis

concept.t: Means-end analysis compares the current state with the goal state, finds the biggest difference and picks an action to shrink it, repeating until the goal is reached.
Allen Newell and Herbert Simon built it into their General Problem Solver computer program; the Tower of Hanoi puzzle is a classic example.
It is a heuristic that often creates subgoals, but its defining feature is reducing the gap between where you are and where you want to be.

wrong.1: Heuristics are the broad family of rule-of-thumb shortcuts; means-end analysis is one specific heuristic, so this answer is too general.
wrong.2: Setting subgoals breaks a problem into smaller steps; it is used within means-end analysis but does not itself compare current and goal states.
wrong.4: Brainstorming (Alex Osborn) generates many ideas without criticism, usually in a group; it does not measure the gap to a goal.

q: According to the Decision Stage Model, how many steps are comprised in taking a decision?
doubt: 'Decision Stage Model' is not a fixed textbook name; Herbert Simon's three phases (intelligence, design, choice) would give (1), and a four-stage group model (orientation, discussion, decision, implementation) would give (2).
who: Irving Janis and Leon Mann, decision-making model (1977)

concept.t: Irving Janis and Leon Mann described sound decision-making as passing through five stages.
(1) Appraising the challenge → (2) surveying alternatives → (3) weighing alternatives → (4) deliberating about commitment → (5) adhering despite negative feedback.
Janis and Mann also named vigilance as the ideal coping pattern, in contrast to defensive avoidance and hypervigilance (panic).

wrong.1: Three matches Herbert Simon's intelligence, design and choice phases, not the five-stage decision model.
wrong.2: Four is the count in some group decision models (orientation, discussion, decision, implementation), not in the five-stage decision model.
wrong.4: Six steps describe the rational decision-making model of organisational behaviour texts, not the five-stage psychological model.

q: Which of the following explains the tendency of traits that are encoded on the same chromosome to be inherited together?
who: Genetic linkage (Thomas Hunt Morgan, fruit flies)

concept.t: Genes that lie close together on the same chromosome tend to be passed on as a unit; this is called linkage.
During meiosis, crossing over can separate linked genes. The closer two genes are, the less often they are split, so the more often they are inherited together.
Linkage is an exception to Gregor Mendel's law of independent assortment, which holds for genes on different chromosomes or far apart on one.

wrong.1: Mitosis is ordinary cell division that produces two identical body cells; it does not explain which traits travel together across generations.
wrong.2: Meiosis forms sex cells and is when assortment happens, but the tendency of same-chromosome genes to stay together is called linkage.
wrong.4: Gene expression is the process by which a gene's code is turned into a protein and becomes active; it does not explain inheritance patterns.

q:
Arrange the following in temporal sequence. 
 
 (a) Establishment of Psychology department in Mysore

 (b) Establishment of Psychology department in Calcutta

 (c) Establishment of Psychology department in Madras

 (d) Establishment of Psychology department in Pune

 (e) First Indian Journal of Psychology

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Narendra Nath Sengupta; history of psychology in India

concept.t: (b) Calcutta University (1915, the first in India) → (a) Mysore (1924) → (e) Indian Journal of Psychology (1926) → (c) Madras → (d) Pune.
Narendra Nath Sengupta set up the first experimental psychology department and laboratory at Calcutta University. M. V. Gopalaswamy started psychology at Mysore.
The Indian Psychological Association was formed in 1925 and launched the Indian Journal of Psychology in 1926. Departments at Madras and Pune came later.

wrong.1: Puts Madras before the Indian Journal of Psychology; the journal (1926) came first, before the Madras department was set up.
wrong.3: Places Madras before Mysore and the journal last; Mysore (1924) and the journal (1926) both came before Madras and Pune.
wrong.4: Starts with Mysore, but Calcutta University had the first psychology department in India, before Mysore.

q: Choose the odd one for the pattern of sympathetic activation during emotions.
who: Walter Cannon, sympathetic fight-or-flight response

concept.t: In emotion the sympathetic branch dilates the pupils to let in more light. Pupil constriction is a parasympathetic effect, so it is the odd one out.
The sympathetic system prepares the body for fight or flight: faster heart and breathing, more sweating, blood sent to the muscles, digestion slowed.
Lowered skin resistance means more sweat on the skin; this is the galvanic skin response recorded by the polygraph.

wrong.1: A faster heartbeat pumps more blood to the muscles; it is a classic sympathetic sign and fits the pattern.
wrong.3: Faster breathing brings in more oxygen for action; it is a sympathetic effect and fits the pattern.
wrong.4: Sympathetic activation of sweat glands lowers skin resistance (raises skin conductance); it fits the pattern and is what the polygraph records.

q: A psychological currency that permits deviation from the group is called:
who: Edwin Hollander, idiosyncrasy credit

concept.t: Idiosyncrasy credit is the goodwill a member earns by conforming and contributing to the group. It can later be 'spent' to deviate without being rejected.
Leaders and high-status members build up credits over time, so the group accepts their new ideas. A newcomer who deviates early has no credit and is punished.
Edwin Hollander's idea explains how an accepted leader can bring change: first conform, then innovate.

wrong.1: Changing one's behaviour or beliefs to match group norms; it is the opposite of deviating, not a credit that allows it.
wrong.2: Following a direct command from an authority figure, as in Stanley Milgram's studies; it involves no store of credit.
wrong.4: Going along with a direct request (foot-in-the-door, door-in-the-face), often without private agreement; it is not a licence to deviate.

q: Which of the following is excluded from Berkowitz's frustration-aggression hypothesis?
who: Leonard Berkowitz, revised frustration-aggression hypothesis

concept.t: The original 1939 hypothesis of John Dollard, Neal Miller and colleagues said frustration always leads to aggression. Leonard Berkowitz dropped this claim.
Frustration produces negative affect (anger) and a readiness to aggress. Whether aggression follows depends on aggressive cues, learning, social rules and thinking.
In his later cognitive neoassociation model, higher-order thinking (appraisal, attribution) can restrain or redirect the urge to aggress.

wrong.2: Included: norms and fear of punishment can hold back aggression even when a person is frustrated, which the revised view accepts.
wrong.3: Included: frustration can lead to other responses such as withdrawal or problem solving, so aggression is only one possible outcome.
wrong.4: Included: in Berkowitz's cognitive neoassociation model, appraisal and higher-order thinking can override the first aggressive urge.

q:
Choose the correct sequence of events following prolonged stress. 
 
 (a) Corticotropin releasing factor

 (b) Adrenocorticotrophic hormone

 (c) Cortisol

 (d) Immune suppression

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis

concept.t: (a) The hypothalamus releases CRF → (b) the anterior pituitary releases ACTH → (c) the adrenal cortex releases cortisol → (d) prolonged high cortisol suppresses the immune system.
Cortisol raises blood sugar and damps inflammation. That helps in the short term, but when stress lasts it lowers lymphocyte activity and resistance to infection.
This is the slow HPA axis; the fast route is the sympathetic-adrenal medullary system releasing adrenaline. Link it to Hans Selye's general adaptation syndrome.

wrong.2: Starts with immune suppression, which is the end result of the chain; CRF must come first to start the hormonal cascade.
wrong.3: Puts cortisol before ACTH, but the adrenal cortex releases cortisol only after ACTH from the pituitary reaches it.
wrong.4: Starts with ACTH, but the pituitary releases ACTH only after the hypothalamus sends CRF.

q: Imaginal disputation by using the ability of a client to imagine is a method of:
who: Albert Ellis, rational emotive behaviour therapy

concept.t: Imaginal disputation is an REBT technique: the client imagines a troubling event and, while still imagining it, disputes the irrational belief behind the upset.
In rational emotive imagery the client pictures the worst case, feels the unhealthy emotion, then changes the self-talk so it becomes a healthy one (concern instead of anxiety).
Albert Ellis's ABCDE: Activating event, Belief, Consequence, Disputing, Effect. Disputing can be cognitive, imaginal or behavioural.

wrong.2: Existential therapists (Irvin Yalom, Rollo May) confront clients with death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness; they do not use imagery to dispute beliefs.
wrong.3: Gestalt therapy (Fritz Perls) confronts avoidance in the here and now with the empty chair and dialogue; it does not dispute beliefs.
wrong.4: Mindfulness trains non-judgemental awareness of thoughts as they are, rather than arguing with or disputing them.

q: Using Hull's theory, Taylor conceptualized that anxiety is an emotionally based drive and therefore high anxious subjects on Taylor's Manifest Anxiety Scale (MAS) should be conditioned faster than low anxious subjects. The study verified the hypothesis. This provides evidence for:
who: Janet Taylor's MAS; construct validation (Anne Anastasi)

concept.t: The MAS was built on Clark Hull's drive theory. Showing that high scorers condition faster, as the theory predicts, supports the scale as a measure of the construct anxiety-as-drive.
Construct validity is how far a test measures a theoretical trait. It is shown by deriving predictions from the theory and testing them, often experimentally.
Concurrent validity = correlation with a criterion measured at the same time. Convergent validity = high correlation with other measures of the same trait (Campbell and Fiske).

wrong.1: Correlating the MAS with a criterion measured at the same time, such as clinicians' ratings; no theory-based experimental prediction is involved.
wrong.3: Shown by high correlations with other anxiety tests; this study tested a prediction from drive theory, not overlap with other tests.
wrong.4: The prediction was confirmed, so the result supports the scale; lack of validity would follow only if high and low scorers conditioned alike.

q:
During the 1960s, Hoffman and others criticised the college entrance examination and other nationally administered educational tests, and argued that: 
 
 (a) These favour shrewd and nimble witted

 (b) These are over concerned with the expression of skill than the quality of thought behind the answer

 (c) These favour subtle, creative and more profound persons

 (d) These carry a bad effect in recognition of merit.

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Banesh Hoffman, The Tyranny of Testing (1962)

concept.t: Banesh Hoffman argued that multiple-choice tests favour the shrewd and nimble-witted (a) and have a bad effect on education and the recognition of merit (d).

(b) twists his point: he said the tests score only the chosen answer, ignore the quality of thought behind it and neglect skill in expression. (c) is the reverse: he said they penalise the subtle, creative, more profound person.
His attack on the multiple-choice format fed the 1960s debate on standardised testing that Anne Anastasi reviews.

wrong.1: (a) is true, but (d) is also one of Hoffman's charges: that such tests harm education and the recognition of merit.
wrong.3: (c) inverts Hoffman: he said the tests penalise the subtle, creative and profound candidate, not favour them.
wrong.4: (d) is true but (c) is false; Hoffman held that creative, profound thinkers are the ones these tests penalise.

q:
Arrange in sequence the scoring categories for 'Motive to Avoid Success', as given below. 
 
 (a) Non-contingent negative consequences

 (b) Interpersonal engagement

 (c) Relief

 (d) Absence of Instrumental conditioning

 (e) Absence of others

 
 Which of the sequences given below is correct?
doubt: This comes from a niche scoring manual not covered in standard textbooks; option (1), which swaps relief and absence of instrumental activity, is the runner-up.
who: Matina Horner, motive to avoid success (fear of success)

concept.t: The revised, empirically derived scoring system for the motive to avoid success lists its categories in the order given: non-contingent negative consequences, interpersonal engagement, relief, absence of instrumental activity, absence of others.

Matina Horner found that many women, writing stories to the cue 'Anne finds herself at the top of her medical school class', imagined negative consequences of success. She called this fear of success.
Like David McClelland's n Ach, it is scored by coding imagery in TAT-type stories against set categories.

wrong.1: Swaps relief and absence of instrumental activity; in the scoring system relief is listed before absence of instrumental activity.
wrong.2: Starts with interpersonal engagement, but non-contingent negative consequences heads the list of categories.
wrong.4: Runs almost backwards, ending with non-contingent negative consequences, which is the first category listed.

q:
Match the following diseases with their corresponding descriptions. 
 
 List I: (a) Parkinson's Disease; (b) Huntington's Disease; (c) Alzheimer's Disease; (d) Korsakoff Syndrome

 List II: (i) Movement disorder associated with cognitive deficits; (ii) Progressive motor disorder associated with severe dementia; (iii) Progressive decline in memory starting with selective forgetting; (iv) A form of dementia caused by deficiency of vitamin Thiamine

 
 Choose the correct option from those given below:
who: Neurodegenerative and amnesic disorders (John Pinel)

concept.t: (a) Parkinson's = (i) movement disorder with cognitive deficits; (b) Huntington's = (ii) progressive motor disorder with severe dementia; (c) Alzheimer's = (iii) progressive memory decline starting with selective forgetting; (d) Korsakoff = (iv) thiamine deficiency dementia.
Parkinson's: loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra, with tremor, rigidity and slowness. Huntington's: a dominant gene, chorea, ending in severe dementia.
Seen in chronic alcoholism: thiamine (vitamin B1) loss damages the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus, causing amnesia with confabulation.

wrong.1: Swaps Parkinson's and Huntington's and puts thiamine with Alzheimer's; thiamine deficiency causes Korsakoff syndrome, not Alzheimer's.
wrong.2: Gives Huntington's the thiamine link and Korsakoff the motor disorder; Huntington's is genetic chorea, Korsakoff is alcohol-related thiamine loss.
wrong.4: Pairs Alzheimer's with thiamine and Korsakoff with a movement disorder; both are wrong, and Huntington's is a motor disorder with dementia.

q: Arrange the Ego Strengths in correct sequence according to Erikson's stages of development.
who: Erik Erikson, psychosocial stages and basic virtues

concept.t: Hope (trust vs mistrust) → will (autonomy vs shame) → purpose (initiative vs guilt) → competence (industry vs inferiority) → fidelity (identity vs role confusion) → love (intimacy vs isolation) → care (generativity vs stagnation) → wisdom (integrity vs despair).
Erik Erikson called each ego strength the basic virtue that emerges when a stage crisis is resolved well.
Memory aid: 'Hope Will Purposely Compete For Love, Care and Wisdom'.

wrong.1: Puts will last, but will (autonomy vs shame and doubt) is the second virtue, just after hope; wisdom is the final one.
wrong.2: Starts with will and ends with love; hope comes first, and love (intimacy) comes before care and wisdom.
wrong.4: Starts with purpose and puts love last; the sequence begins with hope in infancy and ends with wisdom in old age.

q:
The Generational Digital or Gen D factor: 
 
 (a) pertains to reversal of power hierarchy in terms of digital technology

 (b) pertains to imparting knowledge downward to the younger generation

 (c) calls for psychoeducation of parents and caregivers on digital technology usage

 (d) calls for the adolescent psychoeducation on digital technology usage

 
 Choose the correct option:
doubt: Gen D is a niche term from writing on digital media, not a standard textbook; if (c) is read as a separate recommendation rather than part of the idea, option (1) is the runner-up.
who: Generational digital divide (Gen D factor)

concept.t: The Gen D factor describes a reversal of the usual hierarchy: the young know digital technology better than their parents (a). So the remedy targets the adults: psychoeducation of parents and caregivers (c).

(b) is the traditional direction of teaching; with digital technology, knowledge flows upward from child to parent. (d) misses the point, since the gap lies with the adults who must guide and monitor use.

wrong.1: (a) is right, but the reversed hierarchy is exactly why parents and caregivers need psychoeducation, so (c) also belongs.
wrong.2: Knowledge passing down to the young is the traditional pattern; the Gen D factor describes the reverse, so (b) is false.
wrong.4: Both parts miss the reversal: knowledge goes upward, and the adults, who lag behind, are the ones who need psychoeducation.

q: Involvement of the frontal lobe in intelligence can be understood in terms of which of the following sequences?
doubt: The chain comes from research papers rather than one standard textbook; option (4), with response selection as the frontal step, is the runner-up because the frontal lobe also selects responses.
who: Michael Kane and Randall Engle, executive attention

concept.t: The prefrontal cortex lets a person hold attention on internal representations and block distraction. This controlled attention sets working memory capacity, which in turn predicts general (fluid) reasoning.
Michael Kane and Randall Engle argue that working memory capacity is largely executive attention; John Duncan found lateral frontal cortex active across high-g tasks.
Short-term memory is passive storage; working memory adds active control. That is why working memory tasks correlate more strongly with g.

wrong.2: Response selection is a frontal output function, but the route to reasoning runs through working memory, which this chain leaves out.
wrong.3: Short-term memory is passive storage, not the frontal contribution; the frontal lobe adds attentional control, which turns storage into working memory.
wrong.4: Response selection is a frontal function, but the link from frontal lobe to working memory is internally focused attention, not picking responses.

q: Which of the following are the two major symptoms of Alzheimer's disease?
who: Alois Alzheimer; plaques and tangles

concept.t: The two defining brain signs of Alzheimer's disease are amyloid plaques (clumps of beta-amyloid between neurons) and neurofibrillary tangles (twisted tau threads inside neurons).
Plaques and tangles first build up in the medial temporal lobe (entorhinal cortex, hippocampus), which is why memory goes first. Acetylcholine neurons of the basal forebrain are also lost.
Alois Alzheimer first described plaques and tangles; traditionally a definite diagnosis needs them to be found at autopsy.

wrong.2: Collateral sprouting is regrowth of axon branches after injury, and cerebral ischaemia is loss of blood supply (stroke); neither is an Alzheimer's hallmark.
wrong.3: Plaques are a hallmark, but ischaemia (blocked blood flow) causes stroke and vascular dementia, not Alzheimer's disease.
wrong.4: Tangles are a hallmark, but collateral sprouting is a recovery process after neural damage, not a sign of Alzheimer's.

q:
Which of the following are the advantages of fMRI over PET scan? 
 
 (a) Nothing has to be injected into the body

 (b) Provides both structural and functional information of the same image

 (c) Produces three-dimensional images of activity over the entire brain

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: John Pinel, Biopsychology: fMRI versus PET

concept.t: John Pinel lists the advantages of fMRI over PET: nothing is injected, it gives structural and functional information in the same image, its spatial resolution is better, and it can produce 3-D images of activity over the whole brain. So (a), (b) and (c) are all true.
fMRI tracks the BOLD signal, the rise in oxygenated blood in active areas. PET needs a radioactive tracer injected into the blood.
PET keeps one strength: with labelled ligands it can image specific chemicals and receptors.

wrong.1: (a) and (b) are right, but (c) is also an fMRI advantage Pinel lists: 3-D images of activity across the whole brain.
wrong.2: (a) and (c) are right, but (b) is too: fMRI shows structure and function in the same image, while PET shows only activity.
wrong.3: (b) and (c) are right, but (a) is the most cited advantage: fMRI needs no injected radioactive tracer.

q: Feminist theory helped in:
doubt: Option (4) 'gender issues' is broad and also true; (1) is chosen because challenging gender inequality is the defining aim of feminist theory.
who: Feminist theory and feminist therapy (Gerald Corey)

concept.t: Feminist theory began as a challenge to gender inequality: unequal power, rights and opportunities for women. In therapy its slogan is 'the personal is political'.
Feminist therapists such as Jean Baker Miller look at how gender-role socialisation and oppression shape distress, and aim for an egalitarian therapist-client relationship.
Gerald Corey lists empowerment, valuing women's experience and social change among its goals.

wrong.2: Sexual preferences are studied in sexology and research on sexual orientation; feminist theory centres on power and gender, not sexual preference.
wrong.3: Human development is the field of developmental psychology (Jean Piaget, Erik Erikson); feminists such as Carol Gilligan criticised such theories for male bias but did not build them.
wrong.4: Very broad; feminist theory does deal with gender issues, but its specific contribution is exposing and challenging gender inequality.

q: "Value of behaviour to the organism, its evolutionary history, and its causation in terms of stimulus, hormonal and neurological events" has been an area of study of which of the following?
who: Niko Tinbergen, four questions of ethology

concept.t: Ethology, the biological study of animal behaviour in natural settings, asks about a behaviour's survival value, its evolutionary history and its immediate causes (stimuli, hormones, nerves).
Niko Tinbergen's four questions: causation (mechanism), development, function (survival value) and evolution. Konrad Lorenz and Karl von Frisch shared the 1973 Nobel Prize with him.
Classic ethology terms: fixed action pattern, sign stimulus, imprinting.

wrong.1: Evolutionary psychology (David Buss, Leda Cosmides) explains human mental mechanisms as adaptations; it does not study hormonal and neural causes of animal behaviour.
wrong.2: Sigmund Freud's psychoanalysis studies unconscious conflict and childhood experience, not evolutionary history or hormonal causes of behaviour.
wrong.4: William McDougall's instinct psychology listed inborn instincts as the motives of behaviour; it did not study evolutionary history or neural causation.

q: Which part of the brain is responsible for transferring information from Short Term Memory to Long Term Memory?
who: Hippocampal consolidation; patient H.M. (Brenda Milner)

concept.t: The hippocampus consolidates new information, moving it from short-term into long-term memory.
Patient H.M. (Henry Molaison) lost both hippocampi in epilepsy surgery. His short-term memory and old memories stayed, but he could not form new long-term declarative memories (anterograde amnesia).
Amygdala = emotional memory; cerebellum = motor skills and conditioned reflexes; hypothalamus = drives such as hunger and thirst.

wrong.1: The amygdala adds emotional weight to memories, especially fear; it does not transfer general information into long-term memory.
wrong.2: The hypothalamus regulates hunger, thirst, temperature, sex and the pituitary; it is not the memory consolidation centre.
wrong.4: The cerebellum handles motor coordination, procedural skills and eyeblink conditioning, not consolidation of declarative facts.

q: For becoming a good basketball player, one must use:
who: Heuristics versus algorithms in problem solving

concept.t: Basketball needs split-second decisions in a changing game, so a player relies on heuristics: quick rules of thumb learned from experience, such as 'pass when double-teamed'.
An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure that guarantees a solution but is slow. A heuristic is a shortcut that is fast and usually works, though it can fail.
Gerd Gigerenzer's gaze heuristic (keep the angle of gaze to the ball constant) explains how fielders catch a ball without computing its path.

wrong.1: Algorithms are exhaustive step-by-step procedures that guarantee an answer, as in maths; they are far too slow for fast, changing game situations.
wrong.3: Concepts are mental categories that group objects and ideas; they organise knowledge but are not a strategy for split-second play.
wrong.4: Prototypes are the most typical examples of a concept (Eleanor Rosch); they help with categorising, not quick decisions in a game.

q:
Which of the following correctly describe Nafs (Self or ego) in Sufism? 
 
 (a) It can be viewed along a continuum

 (b) It is not meant to please God

 (c) It refers to negative traits only

 (d) It has a potential to function from the grossest to the highest level

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Sufi psychology: stages of the nafs

concept.t: Sufis see the nafs as a continuum (a) that can rise from the grossest, self-centred level to the highest, purified level (d).

From nafs al-ammara (the commanding self that urges evil) → nafs al-lawwama (the self-reproaching self) → nafs al-mutma'inna (the self at peace), and on to the self that is content with God and pleasing to God.
(b) is false: the higher nafs is pleasing to God. (c) is false: only the lowest level is negative, and the nafs can be refined.

wrong.1: (a) is right but (c) is not; only the lowest level, nafs al-ammara, is negative, while higher levels are calm and pure.
wrong.2: Both are false: the purified nafs is described as pleasing to God, and the nafs is not limited to negative traits.
wrong.3: (d) is right but (b) is not; the aim of Sufi practice is a nafs that is content with God and pleasing to Him.

q:
Match the waves with the corresponding frequencies. 
 
 List I: (a) Alpha waves; (b) Beta waves; (c) Theta waves; (d) Delta waves

 List II: (i) 4–7 Hz; (ii) 14–30 Hz; (iii) 8–13 Hz; (iv) 0–3 Hz

 
 Choose the correct option from those given below:
who: EEG frequency bands (Hans Berger)

concept.t: (a) Alpha = (iii) 8 to 13 Hz; (b) Beta = (ii) 14 to 30 Hz; (c) Theta = (i) 4 to 7 Hz; (d) Delta = (iv) 0 to 3 Hz.
Beta = alert, active thinking; alpha = relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed; theta = drowsiness and light sleep; delta = deep slow-wave sleep.
Frequency falls as arousal falls: beta, then alpha, then theta, then delta.

wrong.2: Swaps alpha and beta; beta is the faster 14 to 30 Hz rhythm of alert thinking, alpha the 8 to 13 Hz relaxed rhythm.
wrong.3: Alpha and beta are right, but theta and delta are swapped; delta is the slowest wave (0 to 3 Hz), seen in deep sleep.
wrong.4: Swaps both pairs: alpha and beta are reversed, and so are theta and delta.

q: Which of the following is the most common anti-obesity hormone?
who: Leptin, the fat-cell satiety hormone

concept.t: Leptin is released by fat cells in proportion to body fat. It acts on the hypothalamus to cut food intake and raise energy use, so it is called the anti-obesity hormone.
ob/ob mice cannot make leptin and become very obese; leptin injections make them eat less and lose weight.
Most obese people have high leptin but are leptin resistant, so leptin does not cure common obesity. Ghrelin from the stomach is the hunger hormone.

wrong.2: Orexin (hypocretin) from the lateral hypothalamus promotes wakefulness and food seeking; its loss causes narcolepsy, and it does not fight obesity.
wrong.3: Insulin from the pancreas lowers blood glucose and promotes fat storage; it also signals satiety, but it is not the main anti-obesity hormone.
wrong.4: Ghrelin is released by an empty stomach and stimulates hunger; it is the hunger hormone, the opposite of an anti-obesity signal.

q:
Arrange the following in sequence as per Atkinson and Shiffrin's model of memory when the information is processed. 
 
 (a) Short term memory

 (b) Elaborative rehearsal

 (c) Long term memory

 (d) Attention (in Sensory memory)

 (e) Sensory memory
who: Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin, multi-store model (1968)

concept.t: (e) Sensory memory holds all input briefly → (d) attention selects part of it → (a) short-term memory → (b) elaborative rehearsal links it to meaning → (c) long-term memory.
Unattended sensory traces fade within about a second (iconic) or a few seconds (echoic). STM holds about 7 ± 2 items for around 20 seconds unless rehearsed.
Maintenance rehearsal keeps an item in STM; elaborative rehearsal (deep processing, Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart) gets it into LTM.

wrong.1: Puts attention before sensory memory; information must enter sensory memory before attention can select any of it.
wrong.2: Puts attention after short-term memory; attention is the gate that moves information from sensory memory into STM.
wrong.4: Same order as option (1): attention cannot come before the sensory register it selects from.

q: Which of the following is the explanation of the Premack principle?
who: David Premack, Premack principle

concept.t: David Premack showed that a high-probability behaviour can reinforce a low-probability one: 'finish your homework, then you can play'.
Reinforcers are treated as activities, not things. Whatever a person prefers to do can be made contingent on a less preferred activity.
Also called Grandma's rule. Its refinement, response deprivation theory, says any activity restricted below its usual level can act as a reinforcer.

wrong.1: Describes a primary reinforcer such as food or water, which satisfies a biological need without any learning.
wrong.2: Describes a secondary (conditioned) reinforcer such as money or praise, which gains value from pairing with primary reinforcers.
wrong.3: Overstates the idea: an activity reinforces only a less probable activity, so reinforcing power depends on relative probability, not on simply being a response.

q:
Arrange in sequence the network of auditory pathways. 
 
 (a) Auditory Nerve

 (b) Cochlear Nuclei

 (c) Superior Olives

 (d) Lateral Lemniscus

 (e) Inferior Colliculi

 (f) Medial Geniculate Nuclei

 (g) Primary Auditory Cortex

 
 Choose the correct sequence:
who: Ascending auditory pathway (Pinel, Carlson)

concept.t: (a) Auditory nerve → (b) cochlear nuclei (medulla) → (c) superior olives → (d) lateral lemniscus → (e) inferior colliculi (midbrain) → (f) medial geniculate nuclei (thalamus) → (g) primary auditory cortex (temporal lobe).
The superior olive is the first point where input from both ears meets, so it compares timing and loudness between the ears to locate sounds.
Medial geniculate = hearing; lateral geniculate = vision.

wrong.1: Puts superior olives before cochlear nuclei and cortex before the medial geniculate; auditory nerve fibres end in the cochlear nuclei first, and the thalamus relays to cortex.
wrong.3: Starts with the cochlear nuclei and puts cortex before the colliculi; the auditory nerve comes first, and the cortex is the final stop.
wrong.4: Lists the pathway backwards, from thalamus to nerve; hearing signals ascend from the auditory nerve to the cortex.

q:
Escalation of commitment involves the following sequence of steps. 
 
 (a) Occurrence of loss

 (b) Self-Justification

 (c) Strengthening by external factor

 (d) Rational expectation of positive outcome

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Barry Staw, escalation of commitment (Greenberg and Baron)

concept.t: (d) A project starts with a rational expectation of a positive outcome → (a) losses occur → (b) the decision maker carries on out of self-justification, not wanting to admit an error → (c) external factors (political pressure, public commitment) strengthen commitment further.
Escalation of commitment is the tendency to keep investing in a failing course of action, 'throwing good money after bad' (Barry Staw).
Remedies: set limits in advance, let different people make the first and later decisions, and review progress regularly.

wrong.1: Puts external pressure before self-justification; the first reaction to early losses is the personal need to justify the decision, with outside forces added later.
wrong.3: Starts with the loss; escalation begins with a sound decision based on a rational expectation of success, before any loss occurs.
wrong.4: Starts with the loss and puts the rational expectation in the middle; the positive expectation comes first and leads to the initial decision.

q: Client: "I really don't have much to say (tapping foot)." Counsellor: "Do you know you are tapping your foot?" Client: "No. I guess I am feeling some impatience (pause). Even more, some confused." Here the counselor is:
doubt: The client's reply does reach a deeper grasp of his feelings, so (4) is defensible, but the counsellor's own move only points out the behaviour, which is awareness work.
who: Fritz Perls, Gestalt awareness technique

concept.t: The counsellor simply points to a nonverbal act the client has not noticed (foot tapping). Bringing an unnoticed behaviour into focus is awareness work.

In Gestalt therapy (Fritz Perls), awareness of what one is doing right now is itself healing. The counsellor reflects the body cue and the client discovers the feeling behind it (impatience, confusion).
Gestalt asks 'what' and 'how' and stays in the here and now; it does not interpret causes or ask 'why'.

wrong.2: The question is gentle and non-judgemental; it neither blames nor attacks the client, so it is not harsh.
wrong.3: Probing the deeper meaning or causes of behaviour is interpretation, as in psychoanalysis; this counsellor does not interpret, the client finds the feeling himself.
wrong.4: The deeper understanding comes from the client, not from any interpretation by the counsellor; the counsellor's own move is only to raise awareness.

q: The Phi-Phenomenon is best seen between which of the following time intervals?
who: Max Wertheimer, apparent motion (1912)

concept.t: When two lights flash one after the other, movement is seen between them when the gap is about 30 to 200 ms, best at about 60 ms.
Gap under about 30 ms: the lights look simultaneous. Gap over about 200 ms: they look successive, two separate flashes. In between, one light seems to move: the phi phenomenon.
Phi is apparent movement, the basis of films and neon signs. Max Wertheimer's study of it, with Wolfgang Köhler and Kurt Koffka, started Gestalt psychology.

wrong.1: Starts above the 30 ms threshold and runs well past 200 ms, where the two flashes are seen as separate (succession), not as movement.
wrong.2: Leaves out the optimal gap of about 60 ms and runs past 200 ms, where the flashes look successive.
wrong.4: Lies almost wholly above 200 ms, where the two lights are seen one after the other with no movement.

q: Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A): Philosophically the word pragmatism emphasizes result rather than methods. Reason (R): A pragmatic view of science accepts a methodological approach to knowledge. In the light of the above two statements, choose the correct option:
doubt: If R is read as pragmatists such as Charles Peirce valuing the method of science, R is true but does not explain A, giving (2).
who: Charles Peirce, William James, John Dewey: pragmatism

concept.t: True. Pragmatism (William James, John Dewey) judges an idea by its practical consequences: what works is true. Results matter more than the route taken.
False as stated. A pragmatic view of science does not commit to one fixed method; it is method-pluralist and uses whatever approach answers the question.
Pragmatism is the usual philosophy behind mixed-methods research: the research question, not the method, comes first.

wrong.1: R is not true as stated, and a stress on a fixed method could not explain a philosophy that puts results ahead of methods.
wrong.2: Needs R to be true; pragmatism does not tie knowledge to one methodological approach, so R fails.
wrong.4: A is the standard definition of pragmatism (truth judged by practical results), so A cannot be false.

q:
Double standards of mental health with regard to adult females: 
 
 (a) depicted adult female behaviour as less socially desirable and healthy

 (b) had set up barriers against the advancement of women in non-traditional roles

 (c) pertain to the changing dual personality of women in the current scenario

 (d) pertain to the identification of the general standards of healthy behaviour with men only

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Inge Broverman and colleagues (1970)

concept.t: In the study by Inge Broverman and colleagues, clinicians rated a healthy woman as less healthy and less socially desirable than a healthy adult, so (a) is true. Such a double standard also discourages women from non-traditional roles, so (b) is true.
Clinicians' picture of a healthy adult (sex unspecified) matched their picture of a healthy man. A healthy woman was seen as more submissive, less independent and more emotional.
(c) 'dual personality' is not part of the concept. The adult standard did match the male one, but (d) alone leaves out the core finding (a), so the best set is (a) and (b).

wrong.1: The adult standard did align with the male one, but (d) alone misses the core finding that female behaviour was rated less healthy and desirable.
wrong.2: (c) is not part of the concept; the double standard is about clinicians' stereotyped judgements, not a changing dual personality of women.
wrong.4: Includes (c), which is false; the double standard concerns stereotyped clinical judgements, not a dual personality of women.

q:
Consider the three types of investigation in psychological research written in alphabetical order: 
 
 (a) Controlled laboratory experiments;

 (b) Ex post facto studies; and

 (c) Field experiment

 
 Arrange them in descending order in terms of their ability to control secondary variance usually.
who: Fred Kerlinger, control of extraneous variance

concept.t: The laboratory experiment controls extraneous (secondary) variance best, the field experiment next, and the ex post facto study least.

(a) laboratory experiment: variables manipulated, setting controlled, random assignment → (c) field experiment: manipulation and randomisation in a real setting with less control → (b) ex post facto: no manipulation, no random assignment.
Fred Kerlinger's MAXMINCON: maximise systematic variance, minimise error variance, control extraneous variance. Control falls as realism rises.

wrong.2: Puts ex post facto second, but it has no manipulation or random assignment, so it controls extraneous variance least, below the field experiment.
wrong.3: A field experiment runs in a natural setting with many uncontrolled influences, so it cannot beat the laboratory experiment.
wrong.4: This is the ascending order (least to most control), the reverse of what is asked.

q:
There are many mnemonic devices to help a person memorize lists of words and vocabulary items. Identify the correct device series. 
 
 (a) Categorical Clustering

 (b) Interactive Images

 (c) Recognition

 (d) Pegword System

 (e) Method of Loci

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Robert Sternberg, mnemonic devices in cognitive psychology

concept.t: Categorical clustering, interactive images, the pegword system and the method of loci are all mnemonic devices; recognition is a way of retrieving, not a device.
Clustering groups items by category; interactive images link items in one vivid scene; pegwords hook items onto rhymes (one is a bun); loci place items along a familiar route.
Other devices: acronyms, acrostics and the keyword system (for foreign vocabulary). Recognition and recall are memory measures.

wrong.1: Includes recognition, which is a retrieval task (picking the right item from choices), not a technique for encoding lists.
wrong.2: Includes recognition, a memory test rather than a mnemonic, and leaves out clustering and the method of loci.
wrong.3: Includes recognition, which is a way of testing memory, and leaves out clustering and interactive images.

q: If you move a book from your desk to a shelf, you know the form of the book is not changing. It may be because of which of the following?
doubt: Moving the book also changes its distance, so size constancy (4) can be argued, but the stem asks about its form, which is shape.
who: Perceptual constancy: shape constancy

concept.t: As you carry the book its image on the retina changes from a rectangle to a trapezoid, yet you still see a rectangle. Keeping form stable is shape constancy.
Perceptual constancy lets us see objects as stable despite changing retinal images: shape, size, brightness and colour constancy.
Shape: form stays the same (an opening door). Size: an object does not seem to shrink as it moves away (a friend walking off).

wrong.1: A monocular depth cue: parallel lines seem to meet in the distance; it signals depth, not a stable form.
wrong.2: A depth cue: the smaller of two similar objects looks farther away; it does not keep form constant.
wrong.4: Keeps an object's perceived size stable as distance changes; the stem asks about form, which is shape constancy.

q:
Arrange the following stages of moral development in sequence of their emergence as an individual grows up. 
 
 (a) Morality of interpersonal cooperation

 (b) Universal ethical principle orientation

 (c) Social order maintaining orientation

 (d) Instrumental Purpose Orientation

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Lawrence Kohlberg, stages of moral development

concept.t: Lawrence Kohlberg's stages run from self-interest to approval to law and order to universal principles: (d) → (a) → (c) → (b).

Stage 2 instrumental purpose (preconventional) → Stage 3 interpersonal cooperation, good boy/nice girl → Stage 4 social order maintaining, law and order (both conventional) → Stage 6 universal ethical principles (postconventional).
Stage 1 is punishment and obedience; Stage 5 is social contract. Three levels, two stages each.

wrong.1: Puts universal ethical principles (Stage 6) before social order maintaining (Stage 4), reversing the last two steps.
wrong.3: Starts with Stage 3 and puts Stage 6 second; instrumental purpose (Stage 2) must come first.
wrong.4: Almost reversed: universal ethical principles is the highest stage, reached last if at all.

q: Beta endorphin is mobilized from the Pituitary Gland during stress in approximately the same quantities as:
who: Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) co-release

concept.t: Beta endorphin and ACTH are cut from the same precursor molecule, pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), in the anterior pituitary, so stress releases them together in roughly equal amounts.
Stress → hypothalamus releases CRF → anterior pituitary splits POMC → ACTH (drives cortisol from the adrenal cortex) plus beta endorphin (pain relief).
This is the basis of stress-induced analgesia: the body's own opioids blunt pain during emergencies.

wrong.2: Made by the hypothalamus, not the pituitary; it triggers the release of ACTH and beta endorphin rather than being released with them.
wrong.3: Released by the adrenal medulla under sympathetic control, not split from POMC in the pituitary.
wrong.4: A neurotransmitter of reward and movement pathways; it is not split from POMC alongside beta endorphin.

q:
Which of the following are the elements of the Language Acquisition Process? 
 
 (a) Phonemes

 (b) Morphemes

 (c) Syntax

 (d) Pragmatics

 
 Choose the correct option:
doubt: All four belong to language development; texts that count pragmatics as an element could support (1), (2) or (4), but the three structural units are the usual set.
who: Structure of language: phonemes, morphemes, syntax

concept.t: A child acquires language by mastering its structural units: phonemes (basic sounds), morphemes (smallest units of meaning) and syntax (rules for ordering words).
Sounds (cooing, babbling) → words made of morphemes → word combinations governed by syntax (telegraphic speech) → full sentences.
Pragmatics is the social use of language (turn taking, politeness); it is about using language in context rather than one of its structural building blocks.

wrong.1: Drops morphemes, the smallest units of meaning, and adds pragmatics, which is the social use of language rather than a structural unit.
wrong.2: Drops phonemes, the basic sound units that babbling and first words are built from, and adds pragmatics instead.
wrong.4: Drops syntax, the grammar rules for combining words, which is central to acquiring language, and adds pragmatics.

q: The core emphasis of developmental psychology is represented by which of these sets of pairs?
doubt: Both (1) and (2) contain stability versus change; (2) works only if the age span is treated as a core issue, which standard texts do not do.
who: Lifespan developmental psychology, core issues

concept.t: Developmental psychology asks how people change and how they stay stable over the lifespan, and which patterns are shared by everyone versus individual to each person.
Shared (normative) pattern: most babies walk around one year. Individual differences: timing and style vary with genes and experience. Stability versus change: does a shy toddler stay shy?
Other core issues: nature versus nurture, continuity versus discontinuity (stages), critical versus sensitive periods.

wrong.2: The age range the field covers is not a theoretical issue; only stability versus change fits here.
wrong.3: Young versus old describes age groups, not a core issue, and the pair leaves out stability versus change.
wrong.4: Research designs (cross-sectional, longitudinal) plus a personality theme; neither pair is the field's core emphasis.

q: Which of the following schools of Buddhism focuses on collective freedom from suffering and feeling the ways of enlightenment?
who: Mahayana Buddhism, bodhisattva ideal

concept.t: Mahayana ('great vehicle') stresses liberation for all beings. Its ideal is the bodhisattva, who delays final nirvana to help others reach enlightenment.
Theravada stresses individual liberation by one's own effort; its ideal is the arhat. Vajrayana is the tantric school of Tibet.
Collective, compassion-based liberation → Mahayana; individual path → Theravada; ritual, mantra and tantra → Vajrayana.

wrong.1: This is the goal itself, the end of craving and suffering, not a school of Buddhism.
wrong.2: The older school of Sri Lanka and South-East Asia; it stresses individual liberation through one's own effort (the arhat ideal).
wrong.4: The tantric school of Tibet using mantras, rituals and a guru; it grew out of Mahayana but is known for esoteric practice.

q: The three psychologists who illustrated the diversity of approaches to functional psychology at Columbia were:
who: James McKeen Cattell, E. L. Thorndike, Robert S. Woodworth

concept.t: At Columbia University functionalism was loose and practical: James McKeen Cattell (mental tests), Edward Thorndike (law of effect) and Robert Woodworth (dynamic psychology).
The formal Chicago school of functionalism was led by John Dewey, James Angell and Harvey Carr.
Robert Woodworth added the organism to S-R, giving S-O-R, and stressed motivation in his dynamic psychology.

wrong.1: Includes Harvey Carr, who led functionalism at Chicago after James Angell, not at Columbia.
wrong.2: Pairs Cattell with two Chicago men: James Angell and Harvey Carr led the Chicago school of functionalism.
wrong.3: Includes James Angell, who made functionalism a formal school at the University of Chicago, not Columbia.

q:
Match the following types of memories with their features. 
 
 List I: (a) Non-declarative memory; (b) Echoic memory; (c) Semantic memory; (d) Episodic memory

 List II: (i) Type of declarative memory containing general knowledge of language and information; (ii) Type of declarative memory containing personal information not readily available to others; (iii) Type of LTM for skills, procedures, habits etc.; (iv) Auditory sensation lasting only for 2 to 4 seconds

 
 Choose the correct option from those given below:
who: Endel Tulving (episodic, semantic); Ulric Neisser (echoic)

concept.t: (a) Non-declarative = (iii) LTM for skills, procedures, habits; (b) Echoic = (iv) auditory sensation lasting 2 to 4 seconds; (c) Semantic = (i) general knowledge of language and facts; (d) Episodic = (ii) personal events not readily available to others.
Declarative (explicit) memory splits into semantic (facts) and episodic (personal events), as Endel Tulving proposed. Non-declarative (implicit) memory covers skills, priming and conditioning.
The iconic (visual) store lasts under a second; the echoic (auditory) store lasts a few seconds. Ulric Neisser named both.

wrong.1: Gives non-declarative memory the semantic definition and echoic memory the episodic one; non-declarative holds skills, echoic is brief auditory sensation.
wrong.2: Pairs non-declarative memory with personal events and echoic with skills; non-declarative holds skills, and echoic is brief auditory sensation.
wrong.4: Pairs non-declarative with auditory sensation and semantic with personal events; non-declarative holds skills, semantic holds general knowledge.

q:
Match the following elements of the Immune System with their respective functions. 
 
 List I: (a) Neutrophils; (b) Immunoglobulins; (c) NK (Natural Killer) cells; (d) CD4

 List II: (i) Yield Marshalls; (ii) Cytotoxic action; (iii) Phagocytic action; (iv) Antibody action

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Psychoneuroimmunology: immune cell functions

concept.t: (a) Neutrophils = (iii) phagocytic action; (b) Immunoglobulins = (iv) antibody action; (c) NK cells = (ii) cytotoxic action; (d) CD4 = (i) marshals that direct the response.
Neutrophils engulf microbes; immunoglobulins are antibodies made by B cells; natural killer cells kill virus-infected and tumour cells; CD4 helper T cells coordinate (marshal) other immune cells.
HIV destroys CD4 cells, so the defence loses its coordinator. Stress also lowers NK cell activity.

wrong.1: Gives neutrophils antibody action and NK cells phagocytosis; antibodies are immunoglobulins and NK cells kill by cytotoxicity.
wrong.2: Calls immunoglobulins marshals and CD4 cells antibodies; it is the reverse: CD4 helper cells marshal, immunoglobulins are antibodies.
wrong.4: Gives neutrophils cytotoxicity and NK cells the marshal role; neutrophils are phagocytes and CD4 cells do the coordinating.

q: Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A): Culture encompasses lifestyles, values, practices and goals which provide distinct identities to people and community. Reason (R): Culture always acts as a constraint in the growth of a community. In the light of the above two statements, choose the correct option:
who: Cultural psychology: culture as a shared way of life

concept.t: True. Culture is a shared design for living (values, beliefs, practices, goals) that gives a group its distinct identity.
False. Culture can limit some choices, but it also enables growth by passing on knowledge, skills and support; 'always a constraint' is wrong.
Absolute words such as always or never in a Reason often signal that it is false.

wrong.1: R is false, since culture also enables growth, and a false Reason cannot explain the Assertion.
wrong.2: Needs R to be true; culture is not always a constraint, it also supports and enables a community's growth.
wrong.4: A is a standard definition of culture, so it is true; R is the false statement.

q: Eleven rural, eleven semi-urban and eleven urban students were thoroughly interviewed and ranked (using a pooled sample of N = 33) for their communication skills. Which one of the following statistical techniques would be appropriate to explore the groupwise difference in communication?
who: Kruskal-Wallis one-way analysis of variance by ranks

concept.t: Three independent groups (rural, semi-urban, urban) with ranked (ordinal) data call for the Kruskal-Wallis H test, the non-parametric version of one-way ANOVA.
Rank all 33 students together, sum the ranks in each group, then H = [12 / N(N + 1)] × Σ(R<sup>2</sup>/n) - 3(N + 1), tested against chi-square with k - 1 = 2 df.
Two independent groups → Mann-Whitney U; related samples → Wilcoxon (two) or Friedman (three or more).

wrong.1: For three or more related (repeated or matched) samples; these are three separate groups of students.
wrong.3: Spearman's rho measures the relationship between two sets of ranks, not differences between groups.
wrong.4: Needs interval scores with roughly normal distributions; ranked data call for its non-parametric version, Kruskal-Wallis.

q: Which of the following norms suggest to people how they ought to behave?
who: Social norms: prescriptive versus proscriptive

concept.t: Prescriptive norms tell people what they ought to do (help a friend, say thank you).
