Proscriptive norms tell people what they ought not to do (do not steal). Together they make up a group's rules of conduct.
Descriptive norms describe what most people actually do; injunctive norms state what is approved or disapproved (Robert Cialdini).

wrong.1: A specific helping norm: help those who depend on us; it is one example of a rule, not the general class of 'ought' norms.
wrong.2: A specific norm (Alvin Gouldner) that we should help, and not harm, those who have helped us; it is one example, not the category.
wrong.4: These say what people should not do, forbidding behaviour rather than suggesting how one ought to behave.

q:
Which of the following are motivators for helping others? 
 
 (a) Attitudes

 (b) Empathy

 (c) Personal distress

 (d) Norms and values

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: C. Daniel Batson, empathy versus personal distress

concept.t: People help out of empathy (concern for the victim), personal distress (to relieve their own upset) and norms and values (social responsibility, reciprocity, moral values). Attitudes are not a standard helping motive.

C. Daniel Batson's empathy-altruism view: empathic concern gives an altruistic motive. Personal distress gives an egoistic motive: help to reduce one's own arousal, as in Jane Piliavin's arousal cost-reward model.
When escape is easy, distressed people often leave instead of helping; empathic people help anyway.

wrong.1: Includes attitudes and drops norms and values, which are classic motives for helping (social responsibility, reciprocity).
wrong.2: Includes attitudes and leaves out personal distress, which Batson showed is a real (egoistic) motive for helping.
wrong.3: Includes attitudes and leaves out empathy, the central altruistic motive for helping.

q:
Suler's (2004) concept of the "Online Disinhibition Effect" is characterised by: 
 
 (a) Anonymity

 (b) Accessibility

 (c) Hierarchies negation

 (d) Easy escape from consequences

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: John Suler, online disinhibition effect (2004)

concept.t: Accessibility is not one of John Suler's factors. Anonymity, the levelling of status and authority (hierarchies negated) and the easy escape from consequences are, so (a), (c) and (d).
Dissociative anonymity, invisibility, asynchronicity (post and leave, an 'emotional hit and run'), solipsistic introjection, dissociative imagination, and minimisation of status and authority.
Disinhibition can be benign (sharing feelings, kindness) or toxic (rude language, threats, flaming).

wrong.1: Includes accessibility, which is not one of Suler's factors, and leaves out the levelling of status and the escape from consequences.
wrong.2: Includes accessibility, which is not a Suler factor, and leaves out the easy escape from consequences that anonymity and asynchronicity allow.
wrong.4: Includes accessibility, which is not a Suler factor, and leaves out the minimisation of status and authority.

q:
A teacher had marks for 50 students in his class. He computed their mean and standard deviation. Considering that the evaluation was too strict, he gave five grace marks to each student. This would: 
 
 (a) Increase mean by five

 (b) Alter standard deviation in an unpredicted way

 (c) Change the rank order of the students

 (d) Change the skewness of the distribution

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Effect of adding a constant to scores

concept.t: Adding the same 5 marks to every score shifts the whole distribution up by 5. The mean rises by 5; nothing else changes.
SD uses deviations from the mean: (X + 5) - (M + 5) = X - M, so the SD is unchanged. Everyone moves up together, so rank order and skewness (shape) stay the same.
Add or subtract a constant: mean changes, SD does not. Multiply by a constant: both mean and SD are multiplied by it.

wrong.2: SD does not change at all, let alone unpredictably, because every deviation from the mean stays the same.
wrong.3: SD and rank order are both unchanged; adding the same amount to everyone keeps the gaps and the order.
wrong.4: Rank order and skewness stay the same; the shape of the distribution only slides along the scale.

q: In quota sampling, the probability of each element of the population being included in the sample:
who: Non-probability sampling: quota sampling

concept.t: Quota sampling is non-probability sampling: interviewers fill set quotas (for example 50 men, 50 women) with whoever they choose, so no one can state each element's chance of selection.
Stratified random sampling also uses subgroups, but picks randomly within each, so probabilities are known. Quota sampling drops that random step.
Known selection probability: simple random, stratified, cluster, systematic. Unknown: quota, purposive, accidental, snowball.

wrong.1: An equal chance equal to the sampling fraction (n/N) holds for simple random sampling, not quota sampling.
wrong.2: Probabilities can be stated in advance only in probability sampling; quota sampling lets the interviewer choose who is included.
wrong.4: A fixed 1/k chance fits systematic sampling, where k is the sampling interval; quota sampling has no known selection probability.

q: "Confrontation" in Gestalt therapies involves:
who: Fritz Perls, Gestalt therapy

concept.t: Gestalt confrontation challenges clients with what and how questions: 'What are you doing now? How are you avoiding?' These keep the client in present awareness.
'Why' questions invite intellectual explanations, excuses and talk about the past, which Fritz Perls saw as a way of avoiding experience.
Gestalt = here and now, awareness, unfinished business, empty chair; confrontation is done in a caring, inviting way.

wrong.1: Gestalt therapists avoid 'why' questions because they lead to intellectualising and explaining away feelings.
wrong.3: Includes 'why', which Gestalt avoids because it pulls the client into rationalising rather than present experience.
wrong.4: Adds 'why', the one question type Gestalt confrontation deliberately avoids.

q: In terms of psychoanalytic therapy, the means of keeping the unconscious conflict intact, thereby impeding any attempts to probe into the real sources of personality problems, is known as:
who: Sigmund Freud, resistance in psychoanalytic therapy

concept.t: In psychoanalytic therapy, resistance is anything that works against therapy and keeps unconscious material out of awareness. It keeps the unconscious conflict intact and blocks probing into its real sources.
Resistance shows as missed sessions, lateness, silence, forgetting or changing the topic. The analyst interprets it, because it points to what the client most fears.
Sigmund Freud treated resistance and transference as the main material of analysis; working through them is the core of the therapy.

wrong.1: The basic defence that pushes threatening material into the unconscious; resistance is how that material is guarded during therapy.
wrong.2: The conscious, deliberate pushing aside of a thought, not an unconscious block that operates in therapy.
wrong.3: A general defence that refuses to accept a painful reality, not the therapy-specific term for blocking the probe.

q:
Jensen's level I and level II abilities can be best understood in terms of which of the following? 
 
 (a) Difficulty and complexity of tasks

 (b) Socioeconomic differences

 (c) Racial differences

 (d) Geographical differences

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Arthur Jensen, Level I and Level II abilities

concept.t: Arthur Jensen split abilities by task complexity and linked them to socioeconomic and racial differences, so (a), (b) and (c). Geography played no part.
Level I: simple associative learning and rote memory (digit span). Level II: abstract reasoning and problem solving, close to Charles Spearman's g.
Jensen reported Level I scores to be fairly similar across social classes and racial groups, but Level II scores to differ. These claims remain heavily disputed.

wrong.1: Includes geographical differences, which Jensen did not use, and leaves out the socioeconomic differences central to his Level I and II work.
wrong.3: Leaves out task complexity, the very basis of the Level I (rote) versus Level II (conceptual) split, and adds geography.
wrong.4: Adds geographical differences; Jensen's theory dealt with task complexity, social class and race, not region.

q: Which part of the neuron is covered by the Myelin sheath?
who: Myelination by Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes

concept.t: Myelin wraps the axon in segments, not end to end. Between the segments are bare gaps called nodes of Ranvier, and the axon hillock and terminal buttons are also uncovered.

Myelin is a fatty insulating layer made by Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system and oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system. The impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction), which makes it much faster.
Myelin covers the axon only, and only in parts. Dendrites receive input and are not myelinated. Loss of myelin in the CNS causes multiple sclerosis.

wrong.1: Myelin is interrupted at the nodes of Ranvier and absent at the axon hillock and terminals, so the axon is never covered completely.
wrong.3: Dendrites are the receiving branches of the neuron; they carry graded potentials and are not myelinated.
wrong.4: No part of a dendrite carries myelin; myelin insulates axons only, to speed up the action potential.

q:
Which of the following are the main biases in the attribution process? 
 
 (a) Fundamental attribution error

 (b) Actor-observer effect

 (c) Situational influence

 (d) Self-serving bias

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Lee Ross; Edward Jones and Richard Nisbett

concept.t: The three classic attribution biases are the fundamental attribution error, the actor-observer effect and the self-serving bias, so (a), (b) and (d) are right.

Fundamental attribution error (Lee Ross, 1977): over-weighting personality and under-weighting the situation when explaining others' behaviour. Actor-observer effect (Edward Jones and Richard Nisbett): we blame the situation for our own acts but dispositions for others' acts.
Self-serving bias: we credit our successes to internal causes (ability, effort) and blame our failures on external ones (luck, a hard test).
Situational influence is a type of cause (an external attribution), not a bias. The biases are errors in how we weigh such causes.

wrong.1: Includes situational influence, which is a kind of external cause people attribute behaviour to, not a bias, and drops the self-serving bias.
wrong.3: Leaves out the fundamental attribution error, the best known attribution bias, and adds situational influence, which is a cause, not a bias.
wrong.4: Leaves out the actor-observer effect and counts situational influence, an external cause rather than an error, as a bias.

q:
Which of the following are true as per Brentano's concept of Phenomenology? 
 
 (a) Outer objects can be perceived only

 (b) Mental experiences can be perceived only

 (c) Feelings and willing be combined in one category

 (d) Outer objects can be both perceived and experienced

 
 Choose the best option:
doubt: The statements loosely paraphrase Franz Brentano's inner versus outer perception, with 'experienced' read as 'observed'; if 'outer objects can be perceived only' is taken as true, (2) is the runner-up.
who: Franz Brentano, act psychology (1874)

concept.t: Franz Brentano held that mental acts can only be perceived inwardly, never observed as objects, while outer (physical) objects can be both perceived and observed. He also merged feeling and willing into one class. So (b), (c) and (d).

In Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint (1874), Brentano said psychology studies mental acts, not contents. Every act is intentional: it is directed at an object (I see something, I judge something).
He sorted acts into ideating (presenting), judging, and loving and hating; the last class joins feeling and willing, which is why (c) is true.
Brentano = act psychology, intentionality, inner perception; his student Edmund Husserl founded phenomenology. Wilhelm Wundt = content psychology.

wrong.1: Gets (c) and (d) but omits (b): for Brentano, mental experiences are known only through inner perception and cannot be observed like outer objects.
wrong.2: Pairs (c) with (a), but Brentano did not limit outer objects to mere perception; unlike mental acts, they can also be observed.
wrong.4: Leaves out (c), the surest Brentano claim: he merged feeling and willing into a single class of loving and hating.

q:
In the context of marginalization, it is suggested to adopt the 'Social Empowerment Model' while dealing with LGBTs because: 
 
 (a) it increases this group's collective and personal self-advocacy

 (b) they learn that they can lead "fulfilling and satisfying" lives

 (c) concerns about LGBT are social concerns and not the concern for the individual

 (d) they realise that being gay or lesbian is not a pathological condition

 
 Choose the correct option:
doubt: This comes from a niche counselling source on the social empowerment model; (2) is the runner-up if (b) is treated as a by-product rather than a reason.
who: Social empowerment model, LGBT-affirmative counselling

concept.t: The social empowerment model builds personal and collective self-advocacy (a), helps clients see that they can lead fulfilling lives (b), and rejects the idea that being gay or lesbian is a pathology (d).
Statement (c) is too absolute. The model links individual distress to social oppression, but it still works with the person; it does not say the individual's concerns do not matter.

Marginalised groups face stigma and discrimination. Empowerment approaches move the focus from 'fixing' the client to building power, skills and community support, in line with the 1973 removal of homosexuality from the DSM.

wrong.1: Includes (c), which wrongly says LGBT concerns are only social and not the individual's; the model works at both levels. It also drops (d).
wrong.2: (a) and (d) are right but incomplete: the model also aims to show clients they can lead fulfilling and satisfying lives.
wrong.3: Includes the false statement (c) and misses (a), self-advocacy, which is the core aim of any empowerment model.

q: The phenomenon where bystanders assume that nothing is wrong in an emergency because no one looks concerned is called:
who: Bibb Latané and John Darley, bystander intervention

concept.t: Pluralistic ignorance is when each bystander looks at the others, sees calm faces, and wrongly concludes there is no emergency. Everyone hides their own worry, so the whole group misreads the situation.

In Bibb Latané and John Darley's model, a bystander must notice the event, interpret it as an emergency, take responsibility, decide how to help, and act. Pluralistic ignorance blocks the interpretation step.
In their smoke-filled room study, students alone reported the smoke far more often than students sitting with passive confederates who ignored it.
Pluralistic ignorance = 'Is it an emergency?' Diffusion of responsibility = 'Is it my job to help?'

wrong.1: The feeling that someone else will help because many are present; it blocks taking responsibility, not interpreting the event as an emergency.
wrong.3: Any voluntary act that benefits others, such as helping; it is the outcome bystander research studies, not this error of interpretation.
wrong.4: The overall finding that people are less likely to help when others are present; pluralistic ignorance is one of its causes.

q:
Match the following types of aggression with their description. 
 
 List I: (a) Hostile Aggression; (b) Emotional Aggression; (c) Instrumental Aggression; (d) Thanatos

 List II: (i) An instinctual drive involving aggressive action towards death; (ii) Injury in which the goal is to obtain something of value; (iii) An act stemming from feelings of anger and aimed at inflicting pain; (iv) Injury or harm that is carried out for the explicit goal of hurting someone

 
 Choose the correct option from those given below:
who: Types of aggression; Sigmund Freud's Thanatos

concept.t: (a) Hostile aggression = (iii) act stemming from anger and aimed at inflicting pain; (b) Emotional aggression = (iv) harm carried out with the explicit goal of hurting someone; (c) Instrumental aggression = (ii) injury used to obtain something of value; (d) Thanatos = (i) instinctual drive towards death.
(c)-(ii) and (d)-(i) are unmistakable, and only option 4 has both. Hostile and emotional aggression are near-synonyms: in both, hurting the victim is the goal itself.
Instrumental aggression uses harm as a means to another goal, such as money or status. Sigmund Freud proposed Thanatos, the death instinct, whose energy turned outward becomes aggression.

wrong.1: Pairs Thanatos with deliberate hurting and instrumental aggression with anger; instrumental aggression aims at a reward, and Thanatos is Freud's death drive.
wrong.2: Gives hostile aggression the 'obtain something of value' description, which defines instrumental aggression, and gives instrumental aggression the goal of hurting.
wrong.3: Gets (a) and (b) right but swaps the last two: Thanatos is the death drive (i), and instrumental aggression seeks something of value (ii).

q: In a newly developed adjustment inventory using a 'Yes/No' format, there were some positively worded items ('Yes' response indicating adjustment) and some negatively worded items ('No' response indicating adjustment). Test developers follow this practice to offset the effects of:
who: Acquiescence response set; balanced keying

concept.t: Acquiescence is the tendency to say 'Yes' or agree regardless of content. Mixing positively and negatively keyed items (balanced keying) means a yes-sayer gains on some items and loses on others, so the bias cancels out.
Acquiescence is a response set: a style of answering that distorts scores whatever the item content. It is common in Yes/No and agree/disagree formats.
Acquiescence → balanced keying. Social desirability → forced-choice items matched on desirability, or a lie scale. Faking → validity scales (e.g. MMPI L, F, K).

wrong.2: Deliberately distorting answers to look good or bad; it is detected with validity scales or reduced with forced-choice formats, not balanced keying.
wrong.3: Answering without reading the items; it is detected by infrequency or consistency scales, not offset by reversing item wording.
wrong.4: Answering to appear favourable; reversed items do not stop it because the desirable answer stays obvious. Forced-choice formats and lie scales are used instead.

q:
Which of the following statements are correct? 
 
 (a) Dilthey opposed reductionism

 (b) Dilthey opposed psychophysical parallelism

 (c) Dilthey rejected the positivistic approaches to experimental psychology

 (d) Dilthey rejected the idea of description

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Wilhelm Dilthey, descriptive psychology (1894)

concept.t: Wilhelm Dilthey opposed reducing mental life to elements or physiology (a), rejected the hypotheses of explanatory psychology such as psychophysical parallelism (b), and rejected positivist experimental psychology as the model for the human sciences (c).
Dilthey did not reject description; he called for a descriptive and analytic psychology that describes lived experience as a connected whole (1894).
He split the Naturwissenschaften (natural sciences, which explain) from the Geisteswissenschaften (human sciences, which understand, Verstehen): 'Nature we explain; mental life we understand.'

wrong.1: Includes (d), but Dilthey championed description: his alternative to experimental psychology was a descriptive and analytic psychology of lived experience.
wrong.2: Includes (d), which is false because description was Dilthey's favoured method, and drops (b), his rejection of psychophysical parallelism.
wrong.3: Both statements are true, but the set is incomplete: opposition to reductionism (a) is central to Dilthey's case for the human sciences.

q:
Creativity has been conceptualised in terms of which of the following? 
 
 (a) As person

 (b) As potential

 (c) As process

 (d) As perseverance

 
 Choose the correct option:
doubt: Lists differ by source; if perseverance is counted as a way of conceptualising creativity (as a persistent trait), (4) is the runner-up.
who: Mel Rhodes' four Ps; creativity as potential

concept.t: Creativity is studied as a person (traits of creative people), as a process (stages of creative thinking) and as a potential (a capacity everyone has to some degree). Perseverance helps creative work but is not a way of defining creativity.
Mel Rhodes grouped definitions of creativity into four Ps: person, process, product and press (the environment).
Graham Wallas described the creative process in four stages: preparation, incubation, illumination and verification.
Creativity as potential links to J. P. Guilford's divergent thinking: tests of fluency, flexibility and originality measure creative capacity, not achievement.

wrong.2: Drops person, one of the most standard views of creativity, and adds perseverance, a helpful trait of creative people rather than a conceptualisation.
wrong.3: Drops potential, a standard view (everyone has some creative capacity), and adds perseverance, which supports creative work but does not define creativity.
wrong.4: Includes perseverance; persistence is one trait of creative people, but standard frameworks define creativity as person, process, product, press or potential.

q:
According to social impact theory, the effect of majority on minority rests on three of the following. 
 
 (a) Majority's strength

 (b) Minority's will

 (c) Immediacy

 (d) Number of persons

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Bibb Latané, social impact theory (1981)

concept.t: In Bibb Latané's social impact theory, influence depends on the strength (status, power) of the source, its immediacy (closeness in space and time) and the number of people. So (a), (c) and (d).
Impact = f(S × I × N). Adding sources raises impact, but each extra person adds less than the one before (diminishing returns).
The minority's will is not part of the formula. Minority influence on a majority is explained by Serge Moscovici's idea of consistency.

wrong.1: Includes the minority's will, which is not a factor in social impact theory, and leaves out the number of people, a core factor.
wrong.3: Leaves out the majority's strength (status, power) and adds the minority's will, which the theory does not include.
wrong.4: Includes the minority's will and leaves out immediacy, the closeness of the source in space and time.

q: Given below are two statements, Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Assertion (A): High sensation seekers are inclined to get involved in a variety of thrill-seeking activities. Reason (R): Engagement in thrill-seeking behaviour triggers the release of epinephrine. In the light of the above two statements, choose the correct option:
doubt: If the setter had the popular 'adrenaline rush' account in mind, (1) would be marked; Marvin Zuckerman's theory explains the trait through arousal needs, dopamine and MAO, not epinephrine release.
who: Marvin Zuckerman, sensation seeking

concept.t: True. Marvin Zuckerman defined sensation seeking as the need for varied, novel and intense experiences; high scorers seek thrills such as skydiving and fast driving.
True. Thrilling, risky activity activates the sympathetic nervous system, and the adrenal medulla releases epinephrine (adrenaline).

Epinephrine is released in anyone doing something scary, high or low sensation seeker. Zuckerman linked the trait to an optimal level of arousal and brain chemistry such as low MAO and dopamine, so R does not explain A.

wrong.1: Both are true, but adrenaline release happens in everyone during thrills; the trait itself is explained by arousal needs and dopamine and MAO differences.
wrong.3: R is true: thrilling or frightening activity triggers sympathetic arousal and epinephrine release from the adrenal medulla.
wrong.4: A is true: seeking varied, intense and risky experiences is exactly how Zuckerman defined high sensation seeking.

q:
Match the following leadership styles with their characteristics. 
 
 List 1: (a) Directive; (b) Supportive; (c) Participative; (d) Achievement oriented

 List 2: (i) Leader consults subordinates thereby permitting them to participate in decision making; (ii) Leader sets challenging goals and seeks improvement in performance; (iii) Leader provides specific guidance by establishing work schedules and rules; (iv) Leader establishes good relations with subordinates and satisfies their needs

 
 Choose the correct option from those given below:
who: Robert House, path-goal theory of leadership (1971)

concept.t: (a) Directive = (iii) specific guidance, schedules and rules; (b) Supportive = (iv) good relations and attention to needs; (c) Participative = (i) consults subordinates in decisions; (d) Achievement-oriented = (ii) sets challenging goals and seeks improvement.
In Robert House's path-goal theory, the leader clears the path to goals and raises followers' belief that effort leads to rewards. The best style depends on the followers and the task.
Path-goal theory draws on Victor Vroom's expectancy theory. Directive suits ambiguous tasks; supportive suits stressful or boring tasks.

wrong.1: Gives directive leadership consultation and participative leadership rule-setting; consulting subordinates is participative, and setting schedules and rules is directive.
wrong.2: Shifts the pairs: directive leaders give specific guidance, not challenging goals, and achievement-oriented leaders set challenging goals rather than consult.
wrong.4: Gives directive leadership the relationship role and participative leadership goal-setting; building good relations is supportive, and consulting is participative.

q: Dr. X, as a therapist, felt a sense of complete understanding towards a father client whose children behaved exactly the way his own children used to behave. This is:
doubt: Many would read 'complete understanding' as empathy (1); but understanding drawn from the therapist's own matching life, not the client's frame of reference, is sympathy or over-identification.
who: Carl Rogers, empathy versus sympathy

concept.t: Dr X's understanding comes from his own past, not from the client's frame of reference. Feeling with a client because 'I have been through the same' is sympathy, which shades into over-identification.
Carl Rogers defined empathy as sensing the client's private world 'as if' it were your own, without losing the 'as if' quality. An empathic therapist never assumes complete understanding.
Sympathy can lead the therapist to project his own experience onto the client and miss what is unique in this father's situation. This links to countertransference.

wrong.1: Understanding the client's world from the client's frame of reference while staying separate; claiming complete understanding through one's own experience goes beyond it.
wrong.2: A cognitive error of judging on too little evidence; the item describes a felt emotional closeness, not a hasty inference.
wrong.3: Warmth (unconditional positive regard) and genuineness (congruence) are Rogers' other core conditions; they concern acceptance and honesty, not a feeling of shared experience.

q: Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A): MRI provides images of brain activity rather than brain images. Reason (R): Results in MRI are obtained from the measurement of waves that hydrogen atoms emit when they are activated by radio-frequency waves in a magnetic field. In the light of the above two statements, choose the correct option:
who: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) versus fMRI

concept.t: False. Standard MRI gives high-resolution pictures of brain structure. Images of brain activity come from fMRI (or PET).
True. In MRI a strong magnetic field lines up hydrogen atoms; a radio-frequency pulse knocks them out of line, and the waves they give off as they realign are measured to build the image.
Structure: CT, MRI. Activity: PET, fMRI (the BOLD signal, based on oxygenated blood flow), EEG.

wrong.1: A is false: plain MRI shows brain structure; it is functional MRI that tracks activity through changes in blood oxygen.
wrong.2: A is false, so this cannot be right: structural MRI images anatomy, not activity.
wrong.3: The reverse is true: A is false (MRI shows structure) and R is true (hydrogen atoms emit the measured waves).

q:
Read the following paragraph and answer questions 91 to 95. The experimental psychologist wanted to explore whether noise adversely affects reaction time (RT). She also wanted to explore whether the stress level would moderate the effect of noise. She varied noise at three levels: low (30 decibels), moderate (60 decibels) and high (90 decibels). She varied stress at two levels: low and high. From the initial pool of college students, subjects were randomly assigned to different groups. However, a few subjects could not turn up to the laboratory due to vacation. In all, two hundred and ninety-seven subjects participated in the experiment. Each subject, in each group, was tested for simple RT, disjunctive RT, and choice RT. The theory and preliminary analyses indicated the three types of RT were moderately correlated. The covariance matrices, showing the covariances among the three types of RT, were found to be quite similar for all the groups. The multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) results were computed to explore the group differences in means. As the most common practice is, four test criteria (Pillai's criterion, Wilks' criterion, Hotelling's criterion, and Roy's criterion) were obtained. Among the different results obtained in this work, one interesting finding was that stress moderated the effect of noise level on reaction time.
 Q.91 Which of the following test criteria is more appropriate than the others?
doubt: Wilks' criterion (2) is the most widely reported default and is fine once covariance matrices are homogeneous; Pillai's is preferred here only because the dropouts make the cells unequal.
who: Pillai's trace, robust MANOVA criterion

concept.t: Dropouts left 297 subjects in 6 cells, and 297 ÷ 6 = 49.5, so the cell sizes are unequal. Pillai's criterion (Pillai's trace) is the most robust of the four to unequal n and assumption violations, so it is the safest choice.
All four test whether group centroids differ on the combined DVs. With 1 df (stress, 2 levels) they give the same F; noise and the interaction have 2 df, so the four can differ.

Wilks' lambda: the usual default. Roy's largest root: most powerful when groups differ on one dimension, least robust. Pillai's trace: advised by Barbara Tabachnick and Linda Fidell when cells are unequal, samples small or homogeneity doubtful.

wrong.1: Roy's largest root uses only the first discriminant dimension; powerful when groups differ on one dimension but the least robust, so a poor choice with unequal cells.
wrong.2: Wilks' lambda is the most commonly reported criterion, but it is less robust than Pillai's trace when cell sizes are unequal, as here after the dropouts.
wrong.3: Hotelling's trace (Hotelling-Lawley) behaves much like Wilks' lambda and is less robust than Pillai's trace to unequal cell sizes.

q: The design employed in the above study can best be labelled as:
who: Factorial design with unequal cell sizes

concept.t: Two IVs are crossed, noise (3 levels) × stress (2 levels), giving a 3 × 2 factorial design with 6 cells. With 297 subjects, 297 ÷ 6 = 49.5, so the cells cannot be equal: the design is unbalanced.
Balanced means every cell has the same n. Dropouts (here, students away on vacation) make cell sizes unequal, which complicates the sums of squares and calls for robust tests.
A covariate is a variable measured before treatment and statistically controlled (ANCOVA). The three RT measures are dependent variables, not covariates.

wrong.1: There are six groups, but they come from two crossed factors (noise and stress), so it is factorial; a single-factor design could not test the noise × stress interaction.
wrong.2: Balanced needs equal n in every cell; 297 subjects cannot be split equally into 6 cells (49.5 each), and dropouts are reported.
wrong.4: No covariate was measured or controlled; simple, disjunctive and choice RT are the dependent variables analysed by MANOVA.

q: Which one of the following conclusions can be confidently drawn from the above study?
who: Interaction (moderation) in a factorial design

concept.t: The passage says stress moderated the effect of noise on RT. Moderation means the effect of one IV changes across levels of another, which is a significant noise × stress interaction.
A main effect is the overall effect of one factor averaged over the other; an interaction exists when the lines for one factor are not parallel across levels of the other.
A significant interaction says nothing about whether the main effects are significant. The passage reports only the interaction, so that is all we can conclude.

wrong.1: The passage never reports the main effect of noise; with a significant interaction the main effect may or may not be significant, and would need qualifying.
wrong.2: No result for the main effect of stress is given; stress is said only to moderate the noise effect, which is an interaction.
wrong.4: Only the interaction is reported; claiming all three effects are significant goes beyond the evidence in the passage.

q: The above information suggests that:
who: Homogeneity of covariance matrices (Box's M test)

concept.t: The passage says the covariance matrices of the three RTs were quite similar for all the groups. That is exactly the MANOVA assumption of homogeneity of covariance matrices, so it is satisfied.
It is the multivariate version of ANOVA's equal-variance assumption: each group should have the same variance on each DV and the same covariances between DVs. It is usually checked with Box's M test.
Box's M is very sensitive in large samples, so a strict level such as .001 is often used. If it is violated and cells are unequal, report Pillai's criterion.

wrong.1: The opposite: covariance matrices that are quite similar across groups mean the homogeneity assumption holds, not fails.
wrong.3: The three RTs were moderately correlated, so their covariances are clearly not zero.
wrong.4: Similar covariance matrices also have similar variances on their diagonals, so equal variances are tenable too.

q: Which one of the following reasons best justifies the application of MANOVA in the present work?
who: Rationale for MANOVA: moderately correlated DVs

concept.t: MANOVA is best justified when there are several DVs that are moderately correlated, as the three RTs are here. It tests group differences on their combined pattern and controls the Type I error of many separate ANOVAs.
If the DVs are uncorrelated, separate ANOVAs do the job. If they are very highly correlated, they are redundant (multicollinearity) and MANOVA loses power.
Number of IVs decides whether a design is factorial; number of DVs decides whether the analysis is multivariate. ANOVA: one DV. MANOVA: two or more DVs.

wrong.1: Several groups and more than one IV justify a factorial design, which a factorial ANOVA handles with a single DV.
wrong.2: More than one DV is needed but not enough: uncorrelated DVs could be analysed by separate ANOVAs, so the moderate correlation is the real reason.
wrong.4: Moderation is the interaction term and can be tested by a factorial ANOVA on each DV; MANOVA is not the only way.

q:
Read the following paragraph and answer questions 96 to 100. A leading business school in the city had a view that its students must attain total proficiency in English language usage. As an initial step, the school authorities decided to develop a brief language usage test. The project incharge wrote 30 items. Each item had five alternative answers, one of which was correct. He administered these 30 items to a sample of 250 students. For item analysis, item-remainder correlations were computed. The item analysis retained 25 items. The twenty-five item version was administered to a fresh sample of 300 students. Three reliability coefficients were computed: split-half reliability coefficient, Kuder-Richardson (K-R) reliability coefficient, and Cronbach alpha. The Cronbach alpha was found to be 0.7. The test-retest reliability was also computed with a time-interval of eight weeks in two administrations, using the same sample. The test-retest correlation was found to be 0.26, significant at the .001 level. The school authorities, pleased with the efforts of the project incharge, asked him to add similar items and develop a 75-item version.
 Q.96 The above information provides evidence for: 
 
 (a) Unsatisfactory test-retest reliability

 (b) Satisfactory test-retest reliability

 (c) Acceptable internal consistency reliability

 (d) Unacceptable internal consistency reliability

 
 Choose the correct option:
who: Reliability benchmarks (Jum Nunnally's 0.70 rule)

concept.t: A test-retest r of 0.26 is far too low, so (a). Cronbach's α of 0.70 meets the usual minimum for a new test, so (c). Hence (a) and (c).

Shared variance = r² = 0.26² ≈ 0.07, so only about 7% of score variance is stable over eight weeks. Significance at .001 comes from the large N: t = 0.26 × √298 ÷ √(1 - 0.0676) ≈ 4.6, which only shows r is not zero.
Statistical significance is not adequacy. A reliability of about 0.70 is acceptable for early research (Jum Nunnally), while good ability tests usually show test-retest coefficients of 0.80 or more.

wrong.2: (a) is right, but α = 0.70 is at the accepted minimum for a new test, so internal consistency is acceptable, not unacceptable.
wrong.3: r = 0.26 explains only about 7% of variance; its significance reflects the large sample of 300, not satisfactory stability.
wrong.4: Both parts are reversed: test-retest r = 0.26 is unsatisfactory, and α = 0.70 is acceptable.

q: Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A): The computation of K-R reliability is questionable in the above study. Reason (R): K-R reliability is suitable for tests with dichotomous items. In the light of the above two statements, choose the correct option:
who: G. Frederic Kuder and Marion Richardson (1937), KR-20

concept.t: False. Each item has five options but only one is correct, so it is scored right = 1, wrong = 0. Every item is therefore dichotomous, and K-R is exactly the right formula.
True. KR-20 (and KR-21) were built for items scored 0/1: KR-20 = (k ÷ (k - 1)) × (1 - Σpq ÷ sX²), where pq is each item's variance.
The number of answer options does not decide this; the scoring does. Rating-scale or partial-credit items need Cronbach's alpha instead.

wrong.1: A is false: five-option items scored right or wrong are dichotomous, so using K-R here is fully appropriate.
wrong.2: A is false: the number of answer choices does not matter; scoring each item as correct (1) or incorrect (0) makes it dichotomous.
wrong.3: The reverse: R is true (K-R suits dichotomously scored items) and A is false.

q: If the project incharge developed a 75-item version by adding similar items, what would be the expected Cronbach alpha?
who: Spearman-Brown prophecy formula

concept.t: Going from 25 to 75 similar items lengthens the test by a factor of n = 75 ÷ 25 = 3. The Spearman-Brown prophecy formula predicts the new reliability.
Longer tests are more reliable, with diminishing returns, as long as the added items are parallel. Halving the test (n = 0.5) would drop 0.7 to 0.35 ÷ 0.65 ≈ 0.54.

wrong.1: Leaves α unchanged; adding parallel items raises reliability, so tripling the length must push it above 0.70.
wrong.2: This is what doubling gives: (2 × 0.7) ÷ (1 + 0.7) = 1.4 ÷ 1.7 ≈ 0.824. The test is tripled, not doubled.
wrong.4: Overshoots: reaching 0.931 would need a test nearly six times as long (about 145 items); tripling gives 2.1 ÷ 2.4 = 0.875.

q: Which one of the following correlations is most suitable for computing item-remainder correlations?
who: Point-biserial correlation in item analysis

concept.t: An item-remainder correlation relates each item, scored 0/1 (a true dichotomy: right or wrong), with the total of the remaining items, a continuous score. Dichotomous with continuous → point-biserial r.
r<sub>pb</sub> = ((M<sub>p</sub> - M<sub>q</sub>) ÷ s<sub>t</sub>) × √(pq), where M<sub>p</sub> and M<sub>q</sub> are the mean remainder scores of those who passed and failed the item.
The item is removed from the total first, so it is not correlated with itself. This stops the item-total correlation from being inflated, which matters most in short tests.

wrong.1: Tetrachoric r is for two variables both artificially dichotomised from underlying normal continua; the remainder score here is continuous.
wrong.2: Phi is for two true dichotomies, such as pass/fail on two items; it suits item-item, not item-remainder, correlation.
wrong.3: The contingency coefficient C is for two categorical variables in a chi-square table; it does not fit a continuous remainder score.

q: Consider the three reliability coefficients computed in the above study: (a) split-half reliability coefficient; (b) K-R reliability coefficient; and (c) Cronbach alpha. Which one of the following is true in the above context?
who: Lee Cronbach (1951): alpha equals KR-20 for 0/1 items

concept.t: For items scored 0/1, each item's variance is pq, so Cronbach's α reduces exactly to KR-20; both equal 0.70 here. A split-half coefficient depends on how the test is split, so it can differ.
α = (k ÷ (k - 1)) × (1 - Σs<sub>i</sub>² ÷ s<sub>X</sub>²). Put s<sub>i</sub>² = p<sub>i</sub>q<sub>i</sub> for dichotomous items and you get KR-20: (k ÷ (k - 1)) × (1 - Σpq ÷ s<sub>X</sub>²).

Split-half correlates two halves (e.g. odd vs even items) and steps it up with Spearman-Brown. Lee Cronbach showed α is the mean of all possible split-half coefficients, so any single split may be higher or lower.
KR-20 = α for dichotomous items. KR-21 assumes all items are equally difficult and gives a value equal to or lower than KR-20.

wrong.1: Split-half reliability depends on the particular split and can differ; only KR-20 and α are mathematically identical for 0/1 items.
wrong.2: K-R (KR-20) and Cronbach's α cannot differ here: with dichotomous items α reduces exactly to KR-20.
wrong.4: Garbled and wrong: the split-half coefficient is the one that can differ, while K-R and α must be equal for 0/1 items.
